::::{.part label="a."}
The revenue reduction that would result from heat pump customers enrolling in Rate HP rather than Rate 1 depends largely on whether PURA decides to auto-enroll known customers who already have heat pumps ("existing heat pump customers") and are currently overpaying under Rate 1. Customers who currently heat with fossil fuels and choose to install heat pumps in the future ("new heat pump customers") and are automatically switched from Rate 1 to Rate HP at the time of installation would actually produce slightly more revenue for the Company upon enrolling in Rate HP, on average, not less.

1. **Existing heat pump customers**: When Massachusetts rolled out seasonal heat pump rates comparable to Rate HP, its investor-owned utilities auto-enrolled more than 100,000 customers who had received heat pump rebates through Mass Save in the first year.[^1a-ma-stat] If PURA decides to follow suit by asking the Company to auto-enroll every customer who has received a heat pump rebate through Energize CT, as I recommend in my testimony, I estimate that about `{python} num(existing_customers)` of the Company's existing heat pump customers would be switched from Rate 1 to Rate HP in a one-time mass auto-enrollment (see part (b) for details on that estimate). If that enrollment occurs in 2027, the Company would collect **`{python} million(short_existing['dist'])`** less in distribution and **`{python} million(short_existing['tx'])`** less in transmission that year, and approximately the same amount less every year thereafter.

   [^1a-ma-stat]: NEEP, [_Getting the Price Signals Right: Aligning Rate Design With Heat Pump Usage_](https://pub.switch.box/neep_GettingPriceSignals_2026), at 27 (Nov. 2026) ("Any customer that received a heat pump rebate through Mass Save was automatically enrolled. In the first year, this led to more than 100,000 residents enrolling in the rate.") [@neep_GettingPriceSignals_2026].

   These customers who would be auto-enrolled in this scenario already have heat pumps and are presently enrolled in Rate 1. This means they are already overpaying for T&D under Rate 1, by an average of `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year, on a T&D bill of `{python} dollar(post_td_rate1)`. Under Rate HP, they would instead pay an average of `{python} dollar(post_td_rate_hp)` per year.[^1a-existing-bills] Because the Company is presently overcharging these customers every year, the average per-customer revenue reduction of `{python} dollar(overpay)` per year that would result from switching an existing heat pump customer from Rate 1 to Rate HP represents a revenue shortfall that would need to be recouped from other residential customers. Indeed, this is intentional: one goal of Rate HP is to unwind an unfair cross-subsidy that flows from residential customers who already have heat pumps to those who heat with fossil fuels.[^1a-cross-subsidy]

   [^1a-existing-bills]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 23:9–10 (Oct. 21, 2026) (the average fossil-heated customer overpays by `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year), 23 n.19 (their post-heat-pump T&D bill is `{python} dollar(post_td_rate1)` under Rate 1) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]. Their Rate HP bill is the Rate 1 bill less the overpayment, which Rate HP is designed to remove (_id._ at 85:2–7). These T&D bills include the customer charge.

   [^1a-cross-subsidy]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 27:11–13 (a cross-subsidy within a rate class arises when one identifiable group "systematically pays more than their cost of service, and that excess revenue allows the customers of another identifiable group to pay less"), 28:20–21 (heat pump customers' overpayment "contributes directly to a cross-subsidy to electric customers that heat with fossil fuels"), and 29:7–17 (that cross-subsidy "violates intra-class equity" and is "_systematic_, _substantial_, and will continue to _grow with electrification_") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   However, PURA could instead choose to make existing heat pump customers _eligible_ for Rate HP, but without auto-enrolling Energize CT rebate recipients en masse. In that scenario, I would expect an order of magnitude fewer customers to enroll, because each would have to become aware of the rate and take steps to apply on their own. This added friction is why opt-in heat pump rates elsewhere have drawn very little participation: Central Maine Power's seasonal heat pump rate pilot peaked at 3,134 enrolled customers, well under the pilot's 5,000-customer cap, and Con Edison's Steady Use Rate — designed to save a typical heat pump customer roughly \$500 a year — had enrolled only about 500 households as of December 2025, barely 1% of the more than 40,000 heat pumps its customers have installed.[^1a-opt-in]

   [^1a-opt-in]: Me. P.U.C. Docket No. 2022-00152, Central Maine Power Company, _Final Report_, Attachment 1 at 2 (Dec. 5, 2025) (3,134 customers enrolled in the Seasonal Heat Pump rate in December 2024, net of disenrollments) [@cmp_Docket202200152Final_2025]; Me. P.U.C. Docket No. 2021-00325, _Investigation into Transmission and Distribution Utility Rate Design to Promote State Policies_, [_Order Approving Seasonal Rate_](https://pub.switch.box/mepuc_Docket202100325Order_2022a), at 2 (Oct. 26, 2022) (pilot rate "would be available to no more than 5,000 customers") [@mepuc_Docket202100325Order_2022a]; Mona Zhang, ["How NY heat pump users got stuck with higher bills,"](https://pub.switch.box/zhang_HowNYHeat_2026) _E&E News_ (Mar. 3, 2026) (Con Edison: "only about 500 households — barely 1 percent" enrolled in the Steady Use Rate as of December, of "more than 40,000 heat pumps" installed; the rate can reduce winter heating bills "by an average of roughly \$500 a year") [@zhang_HowNYHeat_2026].

 2. **New heat pump customers**: If PURA decides to auto-enroll all customers who currently heat with fossil fuels but choose to install a heat pump in the future, I estimate that between `{python} num(c1.floor_enrolled[1][1] - existing_customers)` and `{python} num(c1.ceiling_enrolled[-1][1] - c1.ceiling_enrolled[-2][1])` customers a year would be auto-enrolled (see part (c) for details on this estimate). Unlike switching an existing heat pump customer, switching a new heat pump customer from Rate 1 to Rate HP at the same time that they install their heat pump _increases_ the revenue the Company collects from that customer, rather than decreasing it.

   That is because customers who choose to install heat pumps in the future are not yet paying an additional `{python} dollar(inc_td)` a year for T&D: they are currently on Rate 1, but they have yet to electrify their heating, so their winter kWh have not gone up yet. Switching them from Rate 1 to Rate HP at the same time that they install their heat pumps (and increase their winter kWh) does not decrease the amount of revenue the Company collects from them — revenue that would need to be collected from other residential customers.

   On the contrary, auto-enrolling these customers onto Rate HP at install time would slightly _increase_ the annual T&D revenue the Company collects from each of them (`{python} dollar(post_td_rate_hp)`, on average) after heat pumps, compared with what they paid under Rate 1 (`{python} dollar(pre_td_with_cc)`) before heat pumps. This is not an accident: Rate HP is purposefully designed so that, on average, customers with heat pumps pay their pre-heat-pump T&D bill, plus an additional `{python} dollar(inc_mc)` to cover the incremental T&D costs their heat pump causes.[^1a-new-bills] Auto-enrolling new heat pump customers would therefore not reduce the total revenue the Company collects from this population. It would increase it.

   [^1a-new-bills]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 23:2–5 (average fossil-fuel heated customer's post-heat pump T&D charges rise `{python} dollar(inc_td)` a year under Rate 1), 20:7–8 (incremental marginal T&D cost of `{python} dollar(inc_mc)` a year), 85:2–7 (Rate HP sets the post-heat-pump T&D bill equal to the pre-heat-pump bill plus that incremental cost) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

Tables 1 and 2 below put these revenue increases and decreases together to give the _net_ change in the Company's distribution and transmission revenue that would result from Rate HP in each of the first five rate years, in millions of dollars, for my low and high estimates of new heat pump customers. Every figure appears on the `revenue` sheet of CIEC-1 Attachment 1 (Excel, formulas intact).[^1a-workbook]

[^1a-workbook]: [CIEC-1 Attachment 1, `CIEC-1a_rate_hp_revenue_reduction.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PpbYFGIe1o-Wqbucw4jIQOzvYSG75kw-/view), sheet `revenue`: the per-customer decrease and increase in rows 4–5, and the low and high estimates year by year below them. The `README` sheet explains each input [@velez_Docket260510CIEC1_2026].

**Notes on Tables 1 and 2**

- The initial mass auto-enrollment of Energize CT recipients is likely to miss some existing heat pump customers, who may voluntarily enroll in the first five years. The number of such customers is likely to be an order of magnitude lower than the number auto-enrolled, but I have no basis for estimating it, so I have left it out. By the same token, if PURA declines to auto-enroll existing heat pump customers, I would expect an order of magnitude fewer of them to voluntarily opt in. In that scenario, the revenue reduction from existing heat pump customers would likely shrink by an order of magnitude or more.
- Assumptions: Both tables assume every customer who has already received a heat pump rebate through Energize CT is auto-enrolled, that every new heat pump customer receives an Energize CT rebate and is likewise auto-enrolled, and that no auto-enrolled customer opts out. Loads and rates are held constant.
- Rate HP would take effect at the start of the Rate Year, July 1, 2027. I number each rate year by the calendar year in which it begins, from 2027 (July 2027 through June 2028) to 2031.
- The customer archetype use to represent both existing and new heat pump custoemrs is the average fossil fuel-heated electricity customer in the Company's territory, the same customer my direct testimony uses to set Rate HP.[^1a-load]
- As in my testimony, switching an existing heat pump customer from Rate 1 to Rate HP reduces the revenue collected from them by **`{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)`** a year: **`{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)`** in distribution and **`{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)`** in transmission, because Rate HP lowers both charges from November through March.[^1a-rates]
- Enrolling a new heat pump customer in Rate HP at the time of installation increases revenue by **`{python} dollar(c1.inc_total, 2)`** a year: **`{python} dollar(c1.inc_dist, 2)`** in distribution and **`{python} dollar(c1.inc_tx, 2)`** in transmission — the incremental marginal T&D cost the heat pump imposes, which Rate HP is designed to recover. The customer archetype for both figures is the average fossil fuel-heated electricity customer in the Company's territory, the same customer my direct testimony uses to set Rate HP.

## CIEC-2

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 95, lines 1-16, and page 98, lines 10-18.

::: {.referenced-testimony}

**Velez Direct, printed p. 95, lines 1–16**

95:1   **Q. Could automatic enrollment cause some heat pump customers to see higher bills?**\
95:2   **A.** No, because Rate HP is specifically designed so that _every heat pump customer pays less than_\
95:3   _they would under Rate 1_. By lowering Rate 1’s existing winter rates, no heat pump customer\
95:4   would be made worse off by being placed on Rate HP.\
95:5   This is the key link between rate design and enrollment. A rate that only _lowers_ charges\
95:6   can be safely applied to all heat pump customers without risk of adverse bill impacts. If the rate\
95:7   raised some charges and lowered others — for example, a higher fixed charge paired with a\
95:8   lower volumetric rate — some customers could see higher bills in certain months. The seasonal\
95:9   winter reduction avoids this entirely: summer rates are unchanged, and winter rates are only\
95:10  lower. There are no structural losers.\
95:11  A rate design that only lowers charges unlocks auto-enrollment, but it necessarily\
95:12  constrains eligibility: it must be a tech-specific rate, rather than one available to all residential\
95:13  customers. A lower rate is justified for heat pump customers. As covered in section III, they are\
95:14  structural “high-usage” customers who would otherwise overpay. A lower rate available to all\
95:15  customers would simply lower the bills of anyone who enrolled, which would create a revenue\
95:16  shortfall under heavy enrollment.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 98, lines 10–18**

98:10  But a tech-specific rate opens an additional lever for reducing overcollection that the\
98:11  default rate (or any rate that must be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a\
98:12  whole) does not have: keep the fixed charge the same, and simply lower volumetric charges.\
98:13  If the overcollection problem arises from the application of volumetric rates _designed for the_\
98:14  _average electric customer_ to a subclass of residential customers with structurally _above-average_\
98:15  usage, then simply lowering the volumetric rates for that population reduces overcollection from\
98:16  that population. Put another way, instead of fundamentally changing the rate design for Rate 1,\
98:17  you can simply recalibrate it, by designing the volumetric rate component for the average heat\
98:18  pump customer, rather than the average residential customer.

:::

::::{.part label="a."}
Please confirm that Rate HP is not designed to be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Please identify who Mr. Velez contends should bear any reduction in distribution and transmission revenue resulting from Rate HP (_e.g._, other residential customers, non-residential customers, or the Company’s shareholders), and explain the basis for that position.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Does Mr. Velez recommend that any portion of the revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP be recovered from customers outside the residential class? If so, identify each class and the amount. If not, explain how his recommendations would prevent that result.

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
In developing his recommendations, did Mr. Velez consider how any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP would be recovered between rate cases through the Company’s reconciling mechanisms? If so, describe that consideration and provide any analysis. If not, explain why not.

::::

:::

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
The term "revenue neutral" is used in many different ways, so I define it precisely here to clarify what my Rate HP proposal does and does not do.

Rate HP is _not_ designed to be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole, in the following sense: if _all_ customers currently on other residential rate schedules were switched to Rate HP — whether or not they had a heat pump — the Company would experience a revenue shortfall.

Rate HP is also _not_ designed to be revenue neutral with respect to residential heat pump customers as a whole, _relative to what they would pay under Rate 1_: under Rate 1, a heat pump customer overpays by `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year, on average, and Rate HP is designed specifically to remove this overcharge, while still charging these customers for any additional T&D costs caused by their heat pump.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
From other residential customers.

My complete proposal _is_ designed to be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole, in the sense that any revenue reduction that occurs when _existing_ heat pump customers who are currently on Rate 1 enroll in Rate HP would be recouped from the residential customers left on Rate 1, by slightly increasing Rate 1's charges. (As shown in CIEC-1(a), any _new_ heat pump customers enrolled in Rate HP at install time would produce more revenue after the switch, not less.)

In other words, the basis for my position that other residential customers should bear any revenue reduction resulting from existing heat pump customers joining Rate HP is this: the Company should have been collecting this revenue from non-heat pump customers in the first place, not from heat pump customers. Rate 1 unfairly shifts costs from non-heat pump customers to heat pump customers; Rate HP unwinds this significant and growing cross-subsidy _within the residential class_ to improve _intra_-class equity.[^inequity]

[^inequity]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 28:20–21 (Oct. 21, 2026) (heat pump customers' overpayment "contributes directly to a cross-subsidy to electric customers that heat with fossil fuels"), 29:7–17 (that cross-subsidy "violates intra-class equity" and is "_systematic_, _substantial_, and will continue to _grow with electrification_"), and 82:5–7 (the "ultimate objective of Rate HP is to fix the intra-class equity and building electrification policy problems that Rate 1 creates") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
No. I recommend that no portion be recovered from customers outside the residential class, because Rate HP addresses an intra-class equity problem.

My recommendations prevent that result by proposing Rate HP as a _residential_ rate schedule, and changing how the residential class's allocated costs are split between Rate 1 and Rate HP, not the cost allocation across classes. So when rates are set, any revenue Rate HP gives up is recovered by slightly raising Rate 1's charges. Nothing moves to other classes. (Reconciling mechanisms work slightly differently; see the following question.)

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
I considered this but did not address it in my testimony. I do so here. The two reconciling mechanisms relevant to Rate HP are the Revenue Decoupling Mechanism (RDM) for distribution and the Transmission Adjustment Clause (TAC) for transmission. Rate HP does not change any other riders — customers on Rate HP pay the same SBC, CTA, FMCC, and SCRAF rates as Rate 1 — so the remaining reconciling mechanisms are unaffected.[^2d-riders]

[^2d-riders]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:1–2 (generation rates, the monthly customer charge, and all distribution riders remain the same as under Rate 1) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

**How the RDM and TAC work.** Between rate cases, the RDM reconciles the Company's actual distribution revenue against the fixed revenue target approved in this proceeding.[^2d-rdm] If actual revenue falls short of the target — because customers used less electricity than forecast, or, in this case, because customers switched to a rate schedule that lowered the per-kWh distribution charges applied to their same usage — the RDM adds a surcharge in the following year to recover the difference. If actual revenue exceeds the target, the RDM credits the difference back. The surcharge or credit is set as a flat ¢/kWh and applied to every rate class.[^2d-rdm-flat] The TAC works similarly for transmission. Each year, it recovers the Company's projected transmission costs (external charges from ISO New England (ISO-NE) that the Company passes through) plus the prior year's under- or over-recovery, and allocates the total among classes by each class's demand at the Company's twelve monthly system peaks rather than by kWh.[^2d-tac]

[^2d-rdm]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 404 (July 14, 2026) (the RDM reconciles "annual authorized distribution revenue with annual actual distribution revenue") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

[^2d-rdm-flat]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-1](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f) at 22:21 ("the rate will be set at a flat kWh rate across all rate classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f].

[^2d-tac]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 409 (the TAC recovers "the difference between the Company's TAC revenue and the Company's TAC costs from the prior period") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h]; Docket No. 26-01-03, _PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company_, [CL&P Rates Filing, Attachment 1, Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) ("RAM Exhibit 4"), at 4:60 (Feb. 17, 2026) (class shares of the transmission revenue requirement are based on "Average rate class KW demands coincident to the Company's 12 monthly system peaks") [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

**New heat pump customers.** When a customer installs a heat pump and enrolls in Rate HP, their electricity consumption rises, with winter kWh roughly tripling. By design, even at Rate HP's lower winter distribution and transmission rates, the volume increase means the Company collects more total revenue from this customer than it collected before the heat pump was installed. As shown in CIEC-1(a), each new heat pump customer enrolled in Rate HP at installation adds roughly `{python} dollar(c13.mean_bill_delta)` a year in T&D revenue above what they paid previously. Between rate cases, this added revenue raises the Company's actual revenue relative to the targets the reconciling mechanisms true up to, pushing them toward a credit.

**Existing heat pump customers.** When an existing heat pump customer switches from Rate 1 to Rate HP, their kWh do not change — they already have a heat pump. They simply pay a lower per-kWh rate in winter. This reduces the Company's distribution and transmission revenue by `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` per customer per year (`{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)` distribution, `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` transmission), as shown in CIEC-1(a).

**At the next rate case.** The shortfall is addressed properly: Rate 1's rates are recalculated without the kWh of the heat pump customers who have moved to Rate HP, and the distribution and transmission revenue shortfalls are recovered from the remaining residential customers, helping to unwind the cross-subsidy between heat pump and non-heat pump residential customers.

**Between rate cases.** Until then, the RDM and TAC reconcile these revenue shortfalls: all else equal, they push each mechanism toward a surcharge in the next Reconciling Adjustment Mechanism (RAM) period, so the Company still recovers its revenue between rate cases.[^2d-ram-timing] That by itself is not a problem. If these mechanisms recovered each class's revenue variance from that class alone, residential customers would bear the shortfall between rate cases just as they would at the next one, and no other class would be affected.

[^2d-ram-timing]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 404 (RDM), 409 (TAC) (each "will be applied as a separate line item on Customer bills for the 12 months beginning approximately 120 days following the annual period subject to reconciliation") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

The problem is that neither mechanism currently works this way. The RDM pools every class's distribution revenue variance and recovers the net through one ¢/kWh rate charged to every class.[^2d-rdm-pooled] The TAC pools the transmission true-up with the current year's transmission revenue requirement and divides the total among classes by their demand at the Company's twelve monthly system peaks.[^2d-tac-pooled] Either way, any shortfall that arises entirely within the residential class leaks to non-residential classes until the next rate case — and vice versa.[^2d-nonres-share]

[^2d-rdm-pooled]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 404 (the RDM Adjustment divides "the difference in the approved distribution revenue target and actual distribution revenue for the preceding annual period" by "the kWh sales anticipated for the 12-month period over which the RDM Adjustment will be applied") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h]; Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-1](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f) at 22:21 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f].

[^2d-tac-pooled]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 409 (the TAC is set by dividing "(1) the current period's Transmission revenue requirement; plus (2) a true-up of any under or over recoveries . . . from the prior year's TAC charges or credits") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h]; [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 1:20, 29, 4:60 [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

[^2d-nonres-share]: Non-residential share of Rate Year billed sales: `{python} num(RDM_TOTAL_MWH)` MWh total billed sales minus `{python} num(residential_mwh)` MWh residential (Rate 1, Rate 5, and Rate 7) = `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` non-residential. Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-2](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g) at 3 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g]; also in [CIEC-2 Attachment 1, `CIEC-2d_rdm_tac_nonres_impact.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eLJvYsvkT8M6AoxvPUtJsZASzt_6Dx4t/view), sheet `inputs`, rows 12–14 [@velez_Docket260510CIEC2_2026].

**Which way the leak runs today.** This leak is not new, and so far it has favored non-residential customers. Every Rate 1 residential customer who installs a heat pump between rate cases contributes more revenue than expected, which flows to the RDM as an over-collection credited to all classes, including non-residential customers. The Authority itself recognized this dynamic: "beneficial electrification will result in increased kWh sales and a net RDM credit to customers."[^2d-pura-rdm] Non-residential classes have been receiving a share of heat pump customers' overpayment for years, and new heat pump customers enrolled in Rate HP would keep that credit flowing.

[^2d-pura-rdm]: Docket No. 23-01-03, _PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company_, [Decision](https://pub.switch.box/pura_Docket230103Decision_2023), at 30 (Aug. 16, 2023) [@pura_Docket230103Decision_2023].

**How large the leak could be.** If PURA chose to auto-enroll the `{python} num(existing_customers)` existing heat pump customers identified in CIEC-1(b), the annual distribution shortfall would be `{python} million(c2d.annual_dist_shortfall)`, and approximately `{python} pct(c2d.nonres_kwh_share)` of it — about `{python} million(c2d.nonres_dist_shortfall)` — would fall on non-residential classes through the RDM until the next rate case. The same dynamic applies to the TAC for the winter transmission rate reduction: about `{python} pct(c2d.nonres_demand_share)` of the `{python} million(c2d.annual_tx_shortfall)` annual transmission shortfall, or `{python} million(c2d.nonres_tx_shortfall)`, would be allocated to non-residential classes by demand — each year, until the next rate case.[^2d-shortfall]

[^2d-shortfall]: `{python} num(existing_customers)` customers × `{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)` distribution and `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` transmission revenue decrease per customer (CIEC-1(a)), times each mechanism's non-residential share: `{python} pct(c2d.nonres_kwh_share)` of billed kWh for the RDM, and `{python} pct(c2d.nonres_demand_share)` of demand at the twelve monthly system peaks for the TAC ([RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 4:18, 20, 56) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026]. [CIEC-2 Attachment 1, `CIEC-2d_rdm_tac_nonres_impact.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eLJvYsvkT8M6AoxvPUtJsZASzt_6Dx4t/view), sheet `shortfall`, rows 6–7; inputs and sources on sheet `inputs` [@velez_Docket260510CIEC2_2026].

Spread over company-wide sales, the distribution shortfall works out to `{python} f"{c2d.rdm_impact_cents_per_kwh:.3f}"` ¢/kWh on every customer's bill.[^2d-rdm-calc] I have not calculated a comparable figure for the transmission shortfall, which the TAC allocates by each class's demand at the Company's twelve monthly system peaks rather than by kWh.

[^2d-rdm-calc]: `{python} million(c2d.annual_dist_shortfall)` annual distribution shortfall ÷ `{python} num(RDM_TOTAL_MWH)` MWh company-wide billed sales (× 1,000 kWh/MWh). [CIEC-2 Attachment 1, `CIEC-2d_rdm_tac_nonres_impact.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eLJvYsvkT8M6AoxvPUtJsZASzt_6Dx4t/view), sheet `shortfall`, row 10 [@velez_Docket260510CIEC2_2026].

These figures are a worst case, however, and most of the shortfall can be avoided.

**Avoiding the existing heat pump customer auto-enrollment reconciliation shortfall.** The shortfall above arises only if existing heat pump customers are auto-enrolled into Rate HP _after_ Rate 1 and Rate HP are set. If the Authority instead sets both rates in this rate case using billing determinants that already place existing heat pump customers' load on Rate HP, then no reconciliation shortfall would arise from those customers. Instead of waiting until the next rate case for a fix, the Authority could address the problem proactively in this rate case.

**Later existing heat pump customer enrollees.** If the Authority auto-enrolls the `{python} num(existing_customers)` existing heat pump customers who received rebates from Energize CT at the start of the rate period, that mass enrollment happens once. Thereafter, the only reconciliation shortfalls would come from existing (not new) heat pump customers who were "missed" by the Company's initial auto-enrollment and who enroll in Rate HP between rate cases. These customers would likely be far fewer in number, because opt-in heat pump rates have achieved negligible participation elsewhere (see my response to CIEC-1(a)).

**Keeping any remainder within the residential class.** For any reconciliation shortfall that remains, PURA has existing regulatory tools that can keep the RDM and TAC from passing it through to non-residential classes, and I recommend that the Authority use them.

One tool is transparency. In June 2026, the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) directed the state's three electric distribution companies, which all offer seasonal heat pump rates, to report "the billed revenues recorded from heat pump customers in their annual revenue decoupling filings and to compare those revenues to the amounts that would have been billed if those customers had not enrolled in the heat pump rates."[^2d-ma-report] In other words: every year, each company must show how much revenue it actually collected from heat pump rate customers and how much it would have collected had those customers stayed on the default rate. That comparison makes the shortfall — or the surplus — visible to the regulator and all parties, rather than burying it in the company-wide RDM true-up. I recommend that the Authority adopt the same reporting requirement here.

Another tool is targeted recovery. If the reporting shows a net shortfall from existing heat pump customers enrolled in Rate HP beyond the amount built into rates, the Authority can direct the Company to recover that amount from the residential class only, rather than spreading it across all classes through the company-wide RDM. There are at least two ways to do this. One is a residential-only adjustment — a separate line item on residential bills that recovers the identified shortfall from the class that Rate HP serves. The other uses the Company's existing RDM Rider, which already contains a provision excluding from the company-wide calculation any revenue "specifically identified and approved for exclusion by PURA."[^2d-rdm-exclusion] The Authority could invoke that provision to exclude the Rate HP shortfall from the company-wide RDM, and instead recover it through a residential-specific mechanism. Either way, the result is the same: the shortfall stays where it belongs — with the class whose rate caused it.

This is not a radical redesign of the RDM. In December 2025, the Authority considered — and declined — a proposal to allocate the entire RDM by class, which would have tracked revenue variances for every rate class separately. The Authority found that approach "indicated significant potential swings to the volumetric rate for certain rate classes" and concluded that "at this time, the current allocation methodology used for the RDM is appropriate."[^2d-rdm-2025] What I recommend is far narrower: it is one identifiable dollar amount, attributable to one rate, assigned to the one class that rate serves. Connecticut's decoupling statute leaves the design of the decoupling mechanism to the Authority, and asks it to consider whether that design is "in the best interest of ratepayers."[^2d-statute] Keeping a residential shortfall with residential customers would meet that test: it shields non-residential customers from a cost they did not cause, and leaves the RDM unchanged for every other class.

[^2d-ma-report]: D.P.U. 25-08-A, _Inquiry by the Department of Public Utilities on its own Motion into a Seasonal Heat Pump Rate_, [Order on Seasonal Heat Pump Rates](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2508Order_2026), at 41 (June 1, 2026) [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

[^2d-rdm-exclusion]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 404 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

[^2d-rdm-2025]: Docket No. 24-12-05, _PURA Procedural Review of the Annual Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company and The United Illuminating Company_, [Decision](https://pub.switch.box/pura_Docket241205Decision_2025), at 22 (Dec. 10, 2025) [@pura_Docket241205Decision_2025].

[^2d-statute]: [Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-19tt(b)](https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_277.htm#sec_16-19tt) ("The authority shall have the discretion to determine the decoupling mechanism and methodology . . . ." and "shall consider factors, including . . . (1) whether the decoupling mechanism and methodology is in the best interest of ratepayers"). I am not an attorney and do not offer a legal opinion. My understanding is that the statute does not require that every revenue variance be spread company-wide; it leaves the choice of mechanism to the Authority.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 83, footnote 75**

Redesigning the retail transmission charge for a specific schedule — e.g., lowering it in winter and raising it in summer to remain revenue-neutral — does not alter the Company’s wholesale transmission obligations or any FERC-jurisdictional rate.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 101, lines 5–17**

101:5   **Q. How could the Company design a seasonal tech-specific heat pump rate correctly?**\
101:6   **A.** Designing a seasonal heat pump rate correctly requires satisfying three conditions:\
101:7     1. The seasonal rate must _lower_ what heat pump customers pay annually. Some seasonal\
101:8         designs try to maintain revenue-neutrality for heat pump customers by lowering the\

101:11    2. The seasonal rate must lower what heat pump customers pay annually _by a sufficient_\
101:12        _amount to eliminate the overpayment_. Reducing the winter rate by 1 c/kWh, for example,\
101:13        would be a half-measure.\
101:14    3. While rates in both seasons can be lowered — the reduced revenue collection doesn’t all\

::::{.part label="a."}
Please explain why Mr. Velez did not propose a revenue-neutral seasonal design under which the winter reductions in Rate HP would be offset by higher summer distribution and transmission rates.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Would Mr. Velez object to a requirement that any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP be recovered solely from the residential class? If so, explain why.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
If any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP were recovered solely from the residential class, please provide Mr. Velez’s estimate of the resulting increase in Rate 1 distribution and transmission charges, with supporting workpapers.

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
I repeat part of my response to CIEC-2(a): Rate HP is _not_ designed to be revenue neutral with respect to residential heat pump customers as a whole, _relative to what they would pay under Rate 1_. Under Rate 1, a heat pump customer overpays by `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year, on average.[^3a-overpay] Rate HP is designed specifically to remove this overcharge, while still charging these customers for any additional T&D costs their heat pumps cause.[^3a-design]

[^3a-overpay]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 23:9–10 (Oct. 21, 2026) ("fossil fuel-heated customers that install heat pumps overpay by an average of \$1,040 a year") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^3a-design]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–7 (the winter rate reductions produce "a population-average T&D bill equal to the customer's pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost of serving the new electrified heating load") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

A revenue-neutral seasonal design would charge heat pump customers `{python} dollar(overpay)` less in winter, only to charge them `{python} dollar(overpay)` more in summer. As my testimony explains, such a design "merely shifts the overpayment between seasons, defeating the entire purpose of a heat pump rate."[^3a-shift]

[^3a-shift]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 101:9–10 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
No. I would welcome it. As explained in CIEC-2(b), such a requirement would make explicit both the rationale and the aim of Rate HP: residential heat pump customers are cross-subsidizing other residential customers, and fair rates can fix this _intra_-class inequity.[^3b-inequity]

[^3b-inequity]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 28:20–21 (heat pump customers' overpayment "contributes directly to a cross-subsidy to electric customers that heat with fossil fuels"), 29:15–17 (that cross-subsidy is "a significant violation of intra-class equity"), and 82:5–7 (the "ultimate objective of Rate HP is to fix the intra-class equity and building electrification policy problems that Rate 1 creates") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
The increase in Rate 1 charges depends almost entirely on whether PURA decides to auto-enroll existing heat pump customers in Rate HP. If PURA directs the Company to auto-enroll every existing customer who has received a heat pump rebate through Energize CT, as my testimony recommends,[^3c-recommend] and the resulting revenue reduction is recovered solely from the residential class, as I propose in CIEC-2(b), Rate 1 distribution and transmission charges would rise by about **`{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['total'], 2)` per kWh** (`{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['dist'], 2)` distribution, `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['tx'], 2)` transmission). That is about **`{python} pct(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['pct_of_td'], 1)`** of Rate 1's proposed `{python} cents(FILED_TOTAL_DEL)` per kWh delivery rate.[^3c-method] However, if PURA decides not to auto-enroll existing heat pump customers who received Energize CT rebates, the increase would likely be an order of magnitude smaller.

[^3c-recommend]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 93:7–12 ("the Company should auto-enroll all known electric customers who have previously installed heat pumps. . . . a portion of these customers are readily identifiable by the Company, those that previously received a heat pump incentive through EnergizeCT or any other relevant state or utility program") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^3c-method]: Net revenue reduction ÷ kWh of residential customers not on Rate HP, in 2031, the year with the highest cumulative enrollment. The estimate is essentially the same in every rate year and under both the low and high estimates of new heat pump customers in CIEC-1(c): `{python} cents(c3.floor_per_kwh['total'])` to `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['total'])` per kWh. Year-by-year figures, both estimates, and all inputs are in [CIEC-3 Attachment 1, `CIEC-3c_rate1_charge_increase.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1n6jLu6muzvLudZ5sVTN2pyl1Di4MdZpW/view) [@velez_Docket260510CIEC3_2026].

This increase is driven entirely by _existing_ heat pump customers, not new ones. As explained in CIEC-1(a), each of the roughly `{python} num(c3.floor_existing)` existing heat pump customers who would be auto-enrolled (CIEC-1(b)) would pay `{python} dollar(c3.dec_dist + c3.dec_tx, 2)` less per year in distribution and transmission charges, on average. The resulting revenue reduction would be recovered from the residential customers who remain on Rate 1.[^3c-per-customer] This is intentional: it is the cost of unwinding a cross-subsidy that currently overcharges residential heat pump customers by `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year, on average.[^3c-cross-subsidy] New heat pump customers, by contrast, do not reduce the Company's revenue when they enroll in Rate HP at installation: each pays `{python} dollar(c3.inc_dist + c3.inc_tx, 2)` _more_ per year in distribution and transmission charges than before the retrofit, on average.[^3c-new]

[^3c-per-customer]: [CIEC-1 Attachment 1, `CIEC-1a_rate_hp_revenue_reduction.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PpbYFGIe1o-Wqbucw4jIQOzvYSG75kw-/view), sheet `revenue`, rows 4–5 (the revenue decrease per existing customer and increase per new customer), and sheet `enrollment`, table "Existing customers" [@velez_Docket260510CIEC1_2026].

[^3c-cross-subsidy]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 23:9–10 ("fossil fuel-heated customers that install heat pumps overpay by an average of \$1,040 a year"), 28:20–21 (that overpayment "contributes directly to a cross-subsidy to electric customers that heat with fossil fuels") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^3c-new]: New customers affect the per-kWh increase only slightly, and only because each one leaves Rate 1, shrinking the kWh over which the existing customers' reduction is recovered. This is why the high estimate of new customers yields a marginally higher increase than the low estimate.

Because the increase comes from existing customers, it hinges on how many of them enroll. If PURA makes existing heat pump customers eligible for Rate HP without auto-enrolling them, I would expect an order of magnitude fewer of them to enroll, because each would have to learn about the rate and apply on their own. That friction is why opt-in heat pump rates elsewhere have drawn little participation, as discussed in CIEC-1(a): Central Maine Power's seasonal heat pump rate pilot peaked at 3,134 enrolled customers, and only about 500 households had enrolled in Con Edison's Steady Use Rate as of December 2025, barely 1% of the more than 40,000 heat pumps its customers have installed.[^3c-opt-in] Without auto-enrollment, the increase in Rate 1 charges would likely shrink by an order of magnitude or more, to roughly `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['total'] / 10, 2)` per kWh or less.

[^3c-opt-in]: Me. P.U.C. Docket No. 2022-00152, Central Maine Power Company, _Final Report_, Attachment 1 at 2 (Dec. 5, 2025) (3,134 customers enrolled in the Seasonal Heat Pump rate in December 2024, net of disenrollments) [@cmp_Docket202200152Final_2025]; Mona Zhang, ["How NY heat pump users got stuck with higher bills,"](https://pub.switch.box/zhang_HowNYHeat_2026) _E&E News_ (Mar. 3, 2026) (Con Edison: "only about 500 households — barely 1 percent" enrolled in the Steady Use Rate as of December, of "more than 40,000 heat pumps" installed) [@zhang_HowNYHeat_2026].

Please confirm that, based on the figures in Velez Direct Testimony, the average fossil fuel-heated customer pays approximately $1,178 per year in distribution and transmission charges ($814 + $364) before installing a heat pump, while causing approximately $123 per year in marginal T&D costs.

::::{.part label="a."}
Confirmed. Before installing a heat pump, the average fossil fuel-heated customer pays `{python} dollar(pre_td)` a year in distribution and transmission charges,[^4a-charges] while causing `{python} dollar(pre_mc)` a year in marginal T&D costs: `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_before)` upstream distribution and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_before)` bulk transmission.[^4a-mc]

[^4a-charges]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 9:3–6 (distribution and transmission charges under Rate 1) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::{.part label="b."}
Confirmed that, before installing a heat pump, the average fossil fuel-heated electric customer pays `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` a year more than the marginal T&D costs it causes. That amount is the customer's contribution to the embedded costs of the existing system (part (c)). Those costs are sunk: no customer's usage today causes them, but they still have to be paid, and nearly every customer pays something toward them.[^4b-sunk] The testimony does not call that contribution an overpayment.

[^4b-sunk]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 13:23–14:2 (existing "infrastructure does need to be paid for, those are _sunk_ costs tied to old investments, not _marginal_ costs") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

Installing a heat pump transfers other customers' embedded costs onto the heat pump customer. Under Rate 1, the customer's T&D charges go up by `{python} dollar(inc_td)` a year, but the heat pump causes only `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` a year in new T&D costs. The remaining `{python} dollar(overpay)` goes toward the existing system, nearly doubling the customer's contribution to it, from `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` to `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate1)`.[^4b-doubles] The existing system costs the same as before, so the heat pump customer has taken `{python} dollar(overpay)` of embedded costs off everyone else, who now pay that much less.[^4b-offset]

[^4b-doubles]: After installing: (`{python} dollar(pre_td)` + `{python} dollar(inc_td)` in added T&D charges) − (`{python} dollar(pre_mc)` + `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` in added marginal T&D cost) = `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate1)`. [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 20:5–8, 23:3–5 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^4b-offset]: The overpayment reaches other customers through two channels. Between rate cases, the RDM credits distribution revenue collected above the approved target back to all rate classes as a flat ¢/kWh, and the TAC trues up transmission revenue to the Company's actual transmission costs (CIEC-2(d)). At the next rate case, the heat pump customer's added kWh, about `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_after - r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` a year for the average fossil fuel-heated home, are spread over the residential class's total kWh, which lowers the per-kWh rates that recover its revenue requirement. [Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h)] at 404 (RDM), 409 (TAC) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

That is why the testimony calls the `{python} dollar(overpay)` an overpayment and not the `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)`: the `{python} dollar(overpay)` is a _transfer_.[^4b-define] The `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` is the fossil fuel-heated customer's pre-existing share of embedded costs, the average amount it paid before installing the heat pump. The `{python} dollar(overpay)` is part of the embedded costs that other customers used to pay, which the heat pump customer takes on without causing any new costs that would justify it. That transfer is what the testimony calls a cross-subsidy, and it violates intra-class equity.[^4b-cross]

The transfer also works directly against state policy: Connecticut has committed to heat pumps making up 65% of residential HVAC sales by 2030 and 90% by 2040, and is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to get customers to switch. But today, Rate 1 charges the average customer who does switch `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year to lower the electric bills of customers who keep heating with fossil fuels.[^4b-policy] And this transfer spoils the economics of switching for gas-heated customers: under Rate 1, only `{python} pct(a.pct_natgas_hp_bill_decrease_default)` would see lower total annual energy bills after installing a heat pump; without the overpayment, `{python} pct(a.pct_natgas_hp_bill_decrease_fair)` would.[^4b-bills]

[^4b-define]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 24:8–10 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^4b-cross]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 27:11–13, 29:7–17 (the cross-subsidy "violates intra-class equity") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^4b-policy]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 34:1–3 (heat pump sales targets), 35:6–9 (Connecticut "is actively spending hundreds of millions of dollars to drive heat pump adoption"), 82:5–7 (the "ultimate objective of Rate HP is to fix the intra-class equity and building electrification policy problems that Rate 1 creates") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^4b-bills]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 40:12–41:2, 41:3–5 (the overpayment is "the single largest barrier to favorable bill outcomes for natural gas-heated customers considering heat pumps") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

**Velez Direct, printed p. 14, lines 1–11**

14:1   infrastructure does need to be paid for, those are _sunk_ costs tied to old investments, not _marginal_\

::::{.part label="a."}
Mr. Velez states that existing T&D infrastructure “does need to be paid for.” Please explain how, under the cost causation framework in Velez Direct Testimony, the embedded costs of existing T&D infrastructure should be recovered and from whom.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
If the incremental usage of a customer is priced at marginal T&D cost, as Mr. Velez proposes for heat pump load, please identify which customers would pay the embedded T&D costs that the incremental usage no longer contributes to.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Does Mr. Velez contend that the incremental load of commercial and industrial customers should likewise be priced at marginal T&D cost? Explain why or why not.

::::

:::

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
The same way they are recovered now. The testimony proposes no change to how embedded T&D costs are recovered, except one: a customer who installs a heat pump keeps paying its pre-heat-pump contribution to those costs, `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` a year for the average fossil fuel-heated customer, plus the `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` a year in new costs its heat pump causes, instead of taking on `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year of other customers' embedded costs, which nearly doubles what it paid toward them before installing the heat pump (CIEC-4(b)).

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Customers who already heat with a heat pump and pay Rate 1 today ("existing heat pump customers") would pay less toward embedded T&D costs under Rate HP, and other residential customers would pay for these costs. This is intentional: these are embedded costs that other customers paid before, and that existing heat pump customers took on when they installed their heat pumps: the overpayment described in CIEC-4(b). Rate HP shifts them back to the customers who paid them originally (see CIEC-2(b)).

Customers who heat with fossil fuels today and install a heat pump after Rate HP takes effect ("new heat pump customers") leave no embedded costs for anyone else to pay. The question assumes their heat pump usage was contributing to embedded costs and would stop. It never was. When rates were set, the customer had not yet installed its heat pump, so that usage is not part of the sales Rate 1 relies on to recover embedded costs. And because the customer moves to Rate HP when it installs the heat pump, Rate 1 never collects embedded T&D costs on that incremental usage in the first place (see CIEC-1(a)). Therefore, after the switch, there is no lost contribution for anyone else to replace. The customer keeps paying its pre-heat-pump contribution under Rate HP, plus the new costs its heat pump causes (see CIEC-4(b)).

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
I take no position. The testimony addresses residential heat pump customers under Rate 1; it did not study the rate designs or load shapes of commercial or industrial customers, and makes no recommendation about how their load should be priced.

Any bill impact comes from customers who already heat with a heat pump and pay Rate 1 today ("existing heat pump customers"). Moving them to Rate HP ends their overpayment and shifts those embedded costs back to the customers who paid them originally (CIEC-2(b) and CIEC-5(b)).

(i) **Residential customers not on Rate HP.** If PURA auto-enrolls existing heat pump customers who have received a heat pump rebate from Energize CT, as my testimony recommends, and the resulting revenue reduction is recovered from the residential class, as I propose in CIEC-2(b), then the average residential customer not on Rate HP would pay about `{python} dollar(c6.ceiling_mean_monthly, 2)` more a month. (ii) **Non-residential customers, including Rates 39 and 57.** No increase, if the Authority adopts the steps I recommend in CIEC-2(c) and (d): setting Rate 1 and Rate HP in this rate case with existing heat pump customers' load already moved to Rate HP, and keeping any later shortfall within the residential class. ::::{.part label="a."}
Please explain why Mr. Velez estimated marginal transmission cost using an avoided Pool Transmission Facility cost and the probability of the New England system peak, rather than the method by which regional and local network transmission costs are actually allocated to the Company.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Please describe Mr. Velez’s understanding of how ISO New England Inc. allocates regional network transmission service costs to the Company, including whether that allocation depends on the Company’s load at the time of the peak in each month.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Has Mr. Velez estimated the effect of heat pump adoption on the Company’s monthly peak loads during November through March, or on the transmission costs allocated to the Company? If so, provide the analysis. If not, explain why not.

Please explain how the 75% reduction in the winter Transmission Service Rate under Rate HP would affect the Company’s recovery of its transmission costs, and identify who would pay any resulting under-recovery.

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
My testimony measures the cost of the new transmission facilities that a heat pump customer's added usage requires. That is a marginal cost. The cost allocation method the question describes measures something else entirely: how the cost of facilities _already built_ is divided among the customers who use them. It cannot tell us what _new_ facilities added load requires.[^7a-embedded]

[^7a-embedded]: _See_ Synapse Energy Economics, [_Avoided Energy Supply Components (AESC) in New England: 2024 Report_](https://pub.switch.box/synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024) ("AESC 2024"), at 285 (May 24, 2024) (the avoided transmission cost does "not include any impact of changes in the cost or cost allocation of already-built regional transmission facilities"), 286 (it "is the value of avoiding or deferring projects associated with load growth") [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024].

The Company did not compute a marginal cost of transmission in this rate case.[^7a-no-mc] I therefore constructed one. An hourly marginal cost has two parts: an annual cost per kilowatt of peak load, and a method for allocating that annual cost to the hours of the year, in proportion to how likely each hour is to fall at the peak that drives new investment. For the annual cost, I used the standard regional estimate. For the allocation to hours, I used the same probability-of-peak method the Company used for its distribution marginal cost. Because the transmission and distribution schedules are built the same way, they can be added together into one hourly marginal delivery cost, which I compared with the delivery charges a heat pump customer pays for its added usage.

The regional estimate is the avoided Pool Transmission Facility cost of \$69/kW-year from AESC 2024: the cost of deferring regional transmission investment by one year through a one-year reduction in peak load.[^7a-aesc] The Company sponsors that study and uses it to screen its own energy efficiency programs, valuing avoided Pool Transmission Facility cost at \$70.0 per kW.[^7a-clm] I inflated the value to 2026 dollars, the dollar year of the Company's marginal cost of service study.[^7a-dollar-year]

[^7a-no-mc]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-026](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("The Marginal cost of transmission was not computed for this rate design.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

[^7a-aesc]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 15:6–9 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [AESC 2024](https://pub.switch.box/synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024) at 283 (the \$69 per kW-year is "the cost of deferring the PTF investment by one year as a result of a one-year reduction in peak load") [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024].

[^7a-clm]: [AESC 2024](https://pub.switch.box/synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024) at 4 (listing "Eversource (Connecticut Light and Power . . .)" among the sponsors) [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024]; CL&P et al., [_2025–2027 Conservation & Load Management Plan_](https://pub.switch.box/clp_20252027Conservation_2024), at 178 ("The electric and fossil fuel avoided costs are based on a regional avoided energy supply cost study completed in 2024 for New England (‘2024 AESC’)") and 181 (Figure 62 lists "Pooled Transmission Facilities" at "\$70.0" per kW, sourced to "2024 AESC," on a "Connecticut counterfactual 1 using a 15-year levelized basis; all values are in 2024 dollars") (Nov. 1, 2024) [@clp_20252027Conservation_2024].

[^7a-dollar-year]: [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 3, Step 1, at 6 [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026].

To allocate that cost to hours, I applied the Company's method to New England system load rather than to the Company's distribution substation load,[^7a-occ733] because Pool Transmission Facilities are regional: as AESC puts it, "the transmission system is built to reliably meet the total system peak, each year."[^7a-regional]

[^7a-occ733]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 15:9–16:3 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 3, Step 2, at 6–7 [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026]; [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-033](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (reprinting the Company's response to OCC-733, which fit the method on "historical hourly Substation Loads from January 2022, to December 2025") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

[^7a-regional]: [AESC 2024](https://pub.switch.box/synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024) at 283 [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Regional Network Service is how ISO New England charges for the region's shared high-voltage transmission system, the Pool Transmission Facilities. ISO New England bills the Company for it every month, and each month's bill depends on the Company's load in a single peak hour of that month, including in November through March.[^7b-031] The bill is built in three steps.

[^7b-031]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-031](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (the costs of "transmission service provided (i.e., billed) to the distribution company . . . are determined on a monthly peak demand basis, at rates determined on a 12-month average peak demand") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

1. **One regional cost pool and one rate.** Each year, the transmission owners' revenue requirements for the Pool Transmission Facilities are added together into a single New England total. That total is divided by the region's load at monthly peaks, averaged over the twelve months of the year, to give a rate per kilowatt-year.[^7b-rate]

   [^7b-rate]: ISO New England, [_Open Access Transmission Tariff, Section II_](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/regulatory/tariff/sect_2/oatt/sect_ii.pdf), at Schedule 9, Lines 1–3 and notes (b)–(c) (the revenue requirement "equals the aggregate of the ATRRs of the PTOs," and the denominator is "[t]he average for the twelve months of the calendar year on which the rate is based of the sum of the coincident Monthly Peaks for all Local Networks") [@isone_OpenAccessTransmission_2026].

2. **One hour per month.** For billing, the tariff divides New England into zones it calls Local Networks, each covering the transmission systems of one transmission owner or group of affiliated owners.[^7b-zones] The Company is in Eversource's zone, which also includes Eversource's systems in western Massachusetts and New Hampshire.[^7b-eversource] Each month, ISO New England finds the hour when the combined load of that zone is highest. That is the only thing the zone does in the calculation: it fixes the hour in which the Company's load is measured.[^7b-load]

   [^7b-zones]: _Id._ at Attachment E (listing each "Local Network of" a named transmission owner or group of companies) (effective Jan. 1, 2023, FERC Docket No. ER23-16-000).

   [^7b-eversource]: Attachment E lists the zone as "[t]he Local Network of the Northeast Utilities companies," Eversource's former name. _Id._ ISO New England, _Open Access Transmission Tariff_, Schedule 21-ES (Part A), at Section 1.5 (the "Eversource Companies" are "The Connecticut Light and Power Company, NSTAR Electric Company (West), and Public Service Company of New Hampshire") (effective Jan. 1, 2022, FERC Docket No. ER20-2054-001).

   [^7b-load]: [ISO New England, _Open Access Transmission Tariff, Section II_](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/regulatory/tariff/sect_2/oatt/sect_ii.pdf), at Section II.21.2 (a customer's billing load is "its hourly load . . . coincident with the coincident aggregate load of all Network Customers served in each Local Network in the hour in which the coincident load is at its maximum for the month ('Monthly Peak')") (effective Sep. 1, 2021, FERC Docket No. ER21-2337-002) [@isone_OpenAccessTransmission_2026].

3. **The Company's bill.** The Company's load in that hour, times the rate, divided by 12, is its bill for the month.[^7b-charge]

   [^7b-charge]: _Id._ at Section II.21.1 (each customer pays "an amount equal to its Monthly Regional Network Load for the month times the applicable Local Network RNS Rate"), Schedule 9 ("Amount to be Paid = ((RNS Rate per kilowatt-year) x (Transmission Customers [sic] Monthly Network Load (a)) x (1/12))").

The monthly peaks therefore decide how the regional cost pool is shared, not how large it is. If the Company's load in a January peak hour rises, the Company pays a larger share of the same pool, and the other utilities in New England pay a smaller one.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
No, for two reasons.

First, an estimate of the transmission costs allocated to the Company would not measure what my testimony measures. My testimony measures the cost of the _new_ transmission facilities that a customer's added load requires (part (a)). A change in the Company's allocation adds no new facilities. As part (b) describes, load at a monthly peak changes the Company's share of the embedded cost of _existing_ facilities.

Second, even if heat pump adoption raised the Company's November–March peak loads, its allocation would not necessarily grow. The Company's share is a ratio: its load at its monthly peaks, divided by the sum of all New England transmission customers' loads at their own monthly peaks. That share rises only if the Company's peak load grows faster, in percentage terms, than the region's. If peak load elsewhere grows as fast or faster, the Company's share stays the same or falls, because the same revenue requirement is spread over more kilowatts. And winter peak load is indeed forecast to grow across all of New England: ISO New England forecasts heat pumps adding to the winter peak in every New England state, 1,600 MW across the region by 2030, of which 224 MW is in Connecticut and 322 MW in Maine.[^7c-isone]

[^7c-isone]: ISO New England, [_Final 2026 Heat Pump Forecast_](https://pub.switch.box/isone_Final2026Heat_2026), at 8 (annual additions to the heat pump stock in each of the six states), 24 (Winter 50/50 Peak Demand by Load Zone: 224 MW for CT, 322 MW for ME and 1,600 MW for ISONE in 2030) (May 1, 2026) [@isone_Final2026Heat_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
Rate HP would not affect whether the Company recovers its transmission costs. The Transmission Adjustment Clause reconciles the Company's transmission revenue against its actual transmission costs, and carries any difference into the next year's rate (CIEC-2(d)).[^7d-tac]

Who would pay any under-recovery depends on which customers enroll, and other responses already answer it:

- **New heat pump customers** cause no under-recovery. Even at the lower winter Transmission Service Rate, each would pay the Company `{python} dollar(c1.inc_tx, 2)` a year more in transmission than it paid before installing its heat pump (CIEC-1(a) and CIEC-6(b)).
- **Existing heat pump customers** would each pay `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` a year less in transmission (CIEC-1(a)). I recommend that other residential customers bear that reduction (CIEC-2(b)), and CIEC-3(c) estimates the resulting increase in Rate 1 charges. Although the Transmission Adjustment Clause is reset every year, what changes each year is the dollars: each annual filing divides each class's share of transmission costs by sales from a fixed past rate year, currently "RY 2020 Billed Sales," not current sales.[^7d-sales] If the billing determinants approved in this rate case place existing heat pump customers' load on Rate HP, Rate 1's transmission rate is set high enough to cover their reduction, and no shortfall arises. If they do not, the reduction becomes a shortfall each year until the next rate case, and each year's true-up would spread part of it to non-residential classes, unless the Authority directs the Company to recover that shortfall from the residential class only, as I recommend in CIEC-2(d).

  [^7d-sales]: [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 4:11–18 [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026]; see also CL&P, Docket No. 25-01-03, [Attachment 1, Exhibits 1–11, to Dave Thompson Rates Testimony](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/DOCKCURR.NSF/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/7f6c517edc6c634185258c310077bf86/$FILE/Docket%20No.%2025-01-03%20-%20Attachment%201,%20Exhibits%201-11,%20to%20Dave%20Thompson%20Rates%20Testimony%20(2.14.25).xlsx), Exhibit 2 at 4 (the same "RY 2020 Billed Sales" a year earlier) (Feb. 14, 2025).

[^7d-tac]: Davis-Parsons Direct, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 409 (the TAC recovers "the difference between the Company's TAC revenue and the Company's TAC costs from the prior period") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

::::{.part label="a."}
Please explain Mr. Velez’s understanding of the basis for the difference between the Rate 5 and Rate 1 Transmission Service Rates, and state whether he contends that difference reflects marginal transmission cost.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Please explain Mr. Velez’s understanding of whether the winter transmission charges in the Massachusetts heat pump rates he describes were designed to recover a winter transmission revenue requirement or were instead set at an estimate of marginal transmission cost.

::::

Please identify any jurisdiction of which Mr. Velez is aware that has set the retail transmission charges for a heat pump rate at an estimate of marginal transmission cost, and provide a copy of the relevant decision or tariff.
