::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
The difference between the Rate 5 and Rate 1 Transmission Service Rates comes from the method the Company uses to divide its transmission costs among its rate class groups. It does not reflect marginal transmission cost, and I do not contend that it does. The Company has not computed a marginal cost of transmission.[^8a-no-mc]

[^8a-no-mc]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-026](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("The Marginal cost of transmission was not computed for this rate design.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

The Company allocates transmission costs by "rate class group." A rate class group is either a single rate class, such as Rate 5, or several rate classes combined.[^8a-groups] Rate 5 (Residential Electric Heating Service) serves homes that use electricity as their primary source of space heat and has been closed to new applicants since December 21, 2006.[^8a-rate5-tariff] For transmission, Rate 5 is a rate class group of its own, and Rates 1 and 7 are combined into another.[^8a-classes]

[^8a-groups]: Docket No. 26-01-03, _PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company_, [CL&P Rates Filing, Attachment 1, Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) ("RAM Exhibit 4"), at 4:11–20 (Feb. 17, 2026) (column headed "12 CP kW Demands by Rate Class," listing Rate 1, Rate 7 and Rate 5 separately) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026]; Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h), at 429 (July 14, 2026) (table of allocators by "Rate Class Group," including "Rate 1 & Rate 7" and "Rate 5") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

[^8a-rate5-tariff]: [Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 246 ("This rate is not available to new applicants after December 21, 2006"; available "only to customers who use electric energy as the primary space heating source") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

[^8a-classes]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-035](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("Rate 7 is included in the cost allocation and overall revenue requirement along with Rate 1") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a]; [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 4:16–20 (Rates 1 and 7 combined, Rate 5 on its own) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

The Company sets each rate class group's Transmission Service Rate in two steps, in its annual Reconciling Adjustment Mechanism filing:[^8a-exh4]

1. **A share of the Company's transmission costs.** The Company divides its total transmission revenue requirement among its rate class groups in proportion to each group's average demand at the Company's twelve monthly system peaks. This follows the way ISO New England bills the Company for regional transmission, based on its load at the peak hour of each month (CIEC-7(b)).
2. **A rate per kWh.** Each rate class group's share is divided by the group's annual sales, taken from a fixed past rate year (CIEC-7(d)), and grossed up for the gross earnings tax.

[^8a-exh4]: [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 4:11–20, 60 (each rate class group's share of the "Transmission & TAC Revenue Target" is its share of "12 CP kW Demands by Rate Class," defined as "Average rate class KW demands coincident to the Company's 12 monthly system peaks," and the rate is that share divided by "RY 2020 Billed Sales," plus gross earnings tax) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

The Rate 5 and Rate 1 rates differ because the two groups' demand at the monthly peaks differs relative to their sales.[^8a-figures]

[^8a-figures]: [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 4:18, 20 (Rates 1 and 7 combined: 1,652,552.5 kW, \$372,620 thousand, 7,916,705 MWh, 5.050¢/kWh with gross earnings tax; Rate 5: 338,287.6 kW, \$76,278 thousand, 1,669,921 MWh, 4.901¢/kWh) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

Rate HP would not be a separate rate class group with its own share of transmission costs, as Rate 5 is. It would sit within the Rate 1 and Rate 7 rate class group, and would change how that group's share is divided among the customers in it (see CIEC-2(c)), not the size of the share relative to other rate class groups, including non-residential customer groups. Existing heat pump customers take service under Rate 1 today, so their demand at the monthly peaks is already counted in the group's share; moving them to Rate HP would leave that demand in the share. New heat pump customers' added demand would count toward the group's share in the same way, whether they took service under Rate 1 or Rate HP.

Moreover, rate classes within the same _group_ can already have different Transmission Service Rates. Rate 7 is in the same group as Rate 1, but instead of Rate 1's 5.050¢/kWh in every hour, Rate 7 customers pay 11.741¢/kWh on-peak and 2.525¢/kWh off-peak.[^8a-rate7]

[^8a-rate7]: [Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 256 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h]; [RAM Exhibit 4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260103Rates_2026) at 2:17, 34 (Rate 7's "Transmission Target" of 5.050¢/kWh, divided into off-peak and on-peak rates using on-peak and off-peak shares of sales that are "set at Rate 1 percentages": 27.4% × 11.741¢ + 72.6% × 2.525¢ = 5.050¢) [@clp_Docket260103Rates_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
My testimony cites Massachusetts as precedent for a commission directing winter transmission reductions in heat pump rates.[^8b-precedent] The Massachusetts winter transmission charges were designed to recover a winter transmission revenue requirement. They were not set at an estimate of marginal transmission cost.[^8b-directed]

[^8b-precedent]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 84:3–12 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^8b-directed]: D.P.U. 25-08-A, _Inquiry by the Department of Public Utilities on its own Motion into a Seasonal Heat Pump Rate_, [Order on Seasonal Heat Pump Rates](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2508Order_2026) ("D.P.U. 25-08-A Order"), at 19 n.4 ("'cost-based' means that the winter transmission charges were structured to be revenue neutral, recovering the capital costs embedded in the transmission service revenue requirement through adjusted winter sales"), 21 (directing National Grid and Unitil to "recover the winter transmission revenue requirement over the adjusted winter sales") (June 1, 2026) [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026]; _see also_ [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 84 n.76 (quoting the same directive) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

The way they recover that revenue requirement, however, rests on the same premise as Rate HP: that the added winter electricity a heat pump uses adds little or no transmission cost. NSTAR Electric's method, which the DPU later directed National Grid and Unitil to follow, has four steps:[^8b-method]

1. Hold the residential class's transmission revenue target constant.
2. Estimate how much electricity the class would use if every residential customer heated with a heat pump. For NSTAR Electric, this nearly tripled winter usage, to 2.86 times its actual level, and slightly reduced summer usage, because heat pumps cool more efficiently than central air conditioners.
3. Set the summer rate so that summer still collects the same revenue as before. Because estimated summer usage is slightly lower, the summer rate rises slightly, from 4.545¢ to 4.890¢/kWh.
4. Divide the revenue that winter collected before by the much larger estimated winter usage.

[^8b-method]: D.P.U. 25-55, [Direct Testimony of Richard D. Chin on behalf of NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) ("Chin Direct"), Exhibit ES-HP-1, at 13:1–12 (winter sales adjusted by "2.86 times the original load," summer by "a nominal adjustment reflecting some efficiency gains over central air conditioning usage"; "The revenue target for Rate R-1/R-2 is held constant to produce revenue neutral seasonal rates"; the current rate "is multiplied against test year sales for the summer period and then divided by the adjusted summer period sales to arrive at a new summer period base distribution rate"), 13:15–19 (transmission rates "calculated in similar fashion to base distribution rates"; the winter transmission price "is then calculated to collect the remaining revenue requirement over the adjusted winter period sales") (Apr. 17, 2025) [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; D.P.U. 25-55, _Petition of NSTAR Electric Company, d/b/a Eversource Energy for Approval of Residential Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2555Order_2025), at 8 (July 29, 2025) [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025]; [D.P.U. 25-08-A Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2508Order_2026) at 21 (directing National Grid and Unitil to design winter transmission charges "consistent with the design of winter transmission charges approved for NSTAR Electric's heat pump rates") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

In other words, the same winter dollars are spread over nearly three times as many kilowatt-hours, so the winter rate falls to about a third of the standard rate. NSTAR Electric's figures show this. Its standard transmission rate was 4.545¢/kWh, and its winter heat pump rate was 1.590¢/kWh, almost exactly 4.545¢ divided by 2.86.[^8b-example] Consider a gas-heated home that uses 1,000 kWh in the winter months and pays \$45.45 in transmission charges on the standard rate. If it installs a heat pump and its winter usage rises to 2,860 kWh, it pays \$45.47 on the heat pump rate: almost exactly the same transmission bill as before, despite nearly three times the usage.

[^8b-example]: [Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) at 10:8 (Table 2) [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]. 4.545¢ ÷ 2.86 = 1.589¢; 1,000 kWh × 4.545¢ = \$45.45; 2,860 kWh × 1.590¢ = \$45.47.

For a typical heat pump household, then, the Massachusetts design adds nothing to the transmission bill for its added winter usage. Rate HP is more conservative: it charges a typical heat pump household the marginal cost of its incremental heat pump load.

The reason for charging heat pump customers less for transmission in winter is also the same as mine: transmission costs are driven by the summer peak. NSTAR Electric explained that transmission costs "are generally set in relation to system peak demand which typically happens in the summer." The DPU agreed that transmission costs are "well-suited to seasonal heat pump rate designs that reflect the timing and manner in which demand-related costs are incurred in a system that is currently summer peaking." It concluded that lowering winter transmission charges in National Grid's and Unitil's heat pump rates "is appropriate based on cost-causation principles and the need to advance the Commonwealth's climate and equity objectives."[^8b-rationale]

[^8b-rationale]: [Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) at 14:12–13 [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; [D.P.U. 25-08-A Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2508Order_2026) at 19, 20 [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026]; _compare_ [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 16:4–5 (distribution and transmission marginal costs "are concentrated entirely in the summer") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

The results are similar too. NSTAR Electric's winter transmission rate was 1.590¢/kWh when proposed, 65% below its annual rate of 4.545¢/kWh. Rate HP's winter transmission rate would be 1.258¢/kWh, 75% below Rate 1's 5.050¢/kWh.[^8b-results]

[^8b-results]: [Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) at 10:8 (Table 2: Rate R-1/R-2 transmission of "\$0.04545/kWh (Annual)"; heat pump rate transmission of "\$0.01590/kWh (All other months)") [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 82 (Table 4) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
I am not aware of any jurisdiction that has set a heat pump rate's retail transmission charge at an estimate of marginal transmission cost. Nor do I propose that Rate HP do so.

Rate HP's winter Transmission Service Rate is not set at marginal cost. It is set so that a customer who switches from fossil fuel heating to a heat pump keeps paying the transmission bill they paid before (which continues to contribute to the embedded cost of the existing transmission system), plus the marginal cost of the load they add.[^8c-calibrated] Only the added load is priced at marginal cost.

[^8c-calibrated]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
Each Massachusetts heat pump rate was designed as if every customer who enrolled were what I call in CIEC-1(a) a "new heat pump customer": a home that heats with fossil fuels, installs a heat pump, and enrolls at the same time. As described in part (b), each company estimated how much electricity its residential customers would use if every one of them switched from gas heating to a heat pump, and set its heat pump rates to collect the residential class's existing revenue target from that usage.[^8d-design] For a new heat pump customer, enrolling does not reduce revenue. Its winter usage rises by about the assumed amount, so it pays about what it paid before installing its heat pump (see the example in part (b)). This is essentially the same dynamic I describe for new heat pump customers under Rate HP in CIEC-1(a), except that under Rate HP they pay slightly more than before, because Rate HP also charges the marginal cost of their added load.

In practice, though, many of the customers who enrolled in Massachusetts were what I call "existing heat pump customers" (CIEC-1(a)): they already had heat pumps under the default rate. Before NSTAR Electric's rates launched, it automatically enrolled every customer who had received a Mass Save heat pump rebate since 2019.[^8d-autoenroll] National Grid likewise automatically enrolled customers who had previously received a Mass Save heat pump rebate.[^8d-ng-autoenroll] NSTAR Electric's net enrollment was 71,490 customers in the rate's first month alone.[^8d-preexisting] Unlike new heat pump customers, existing heat pump customers did not increase their usage when they enrolled, so they now pay less than they did on the standard residential rate. The Massachusetts companies did not raise their standard residential rates to make up that difference, as I propose doing with Rate 1's rates for Rate HP (CIEC-2(c) and CIEC-3(c)). Instead, the difference goes into decoupling. National Grid, for example, states that any shortfall "will be included in the Company's Revenue Decoupling Mechanism."[^8d-rdm]

[^8d-design]: [Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) at 13:4–5 [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; D.P.U. 23-150, _Petition of Massachusetts Electric Company and Nantucket Electric Company, each d/b/a National Grid, pursuant to G.L. c. 164, § 94 and 220 CMR 5.00, for Approval of a General Increase in Base Distribution Rates for Electric Service, a Performance-Based Ratemaking Plan, and a Capital Recovery Mechanism_, National Grid, [Exhibit HP-1, Residential Heat-Pump Rate Implementation Plan](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024) ("National Grid Exhibit HP-1"), at 4 (Dec. 30, 2024) [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

[^8d-autoenroll]: D.P.U. 25-08, [NSTAR Electric Company Response to Information Request DPU-2-4](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket2508Response_2026) (Jan. 23, 2026) ("Before the launch of the rate on November 1, 2025, the Company automatically enrolled all customers who had received a heat pump from a Mass Save Sponsor after January 1, 2019.") [@nstarelectric_Docket2508Response_2026].

[^8d-ng-autoenroll]: [National Grid Exhibit HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024) at 8 ("all customers who previously received a Mass Save heat-pump incentive through the Company or Boston Gas (before the Heat-Pump Rate becomes effective) will be automatically enrolled into the Heat-Pump Rate") [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

[^8d-preexisting]: D.P.U. 26-143, NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, [Revenue Decoupling Adjustment Factor Filing for Effect January 1, 2027](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket26143Revenue_2026) ("NSTAR 2026 RDAF Filing"), at 6 (Oct. 30, 2026; pending) (net enrollment of 71,490 in November 2025; "Customers who enrolled in a heat pump rate may have pre-existing heat pump installations in their homes.") [@nstarelectric_Docket26143Revenue_2026].

[^8d-rdm]: [National Grid Exhibit HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024) at 4 [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

**How the difference is recovered.** Like CL&P's Revenue Decoupling Mechanism and Transmission Adjustment Clause (CIEC-2(d)), the Massachusetts companies' reconciling mechanisms work at the level of the company as a whole, so a portion of the difference is recovered from non-residential customers:

- **Distribution.** All three companies' decoupling mechanisms compare actual base distribution revenue with the target for the company as a whole, then allocate the total over- or under-recovery to every rate class using fixed allocators set in the last rate case. Unitil computes the difference class by class, but then sums the differences "to develop a total Company shortfall or surplus" before allocating it. The allocators assign 39.4% of any shortfall to non-residential classes at National Grid, 49.2% at NSTAR Electric, and 38.8% at Unitil.[^8d-allocators]
- **Transmission.** National Grid and Unitil each track the transmission over- or under-recovery for the company as a whole, add it to the next year's cost forecast, and spread the total across all rate classes by their share of the system peak. National Grid's `$44.4M` under-recovery for October 2024 through September 2025 was allocated this way, with 46.4% going to non-residential classes. Unitil's 2027 transmission balances are spread the same way, with 54.9% going to non-residential classes. NSTAR Electric's tariff folds any over- or under-recovery into the next annual factor and does not limit it to the class that produced it. National Grid's new Heat Pump Transmission Service Charge changes how residential customers are billed, but nothing in its tariff keeps a shortfall in that charge with heat pump customers.[^8d-tsca]

[^8d-allocators]: [National Grid, Revenue Decoupling Mechanism Provision, M.D.P.U. No. 1635](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket2684Exhibit_2026), at 1 (Distribution Revenue Allocator of "Rate R-1/R-2 60.6%"), 3 ("The amount of over- or under-recovery shall be allocated to the rate classes by applying the Distribution Revenue Allocator") (effective Oct. 1, 2026) [@meco_Docket2684Exhibit_2026]; [NSTAR Electric, Revenue Decoupling Adjustment Mechanism, M.D.P.U. No. 60N](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_RevenueDecouplingAdjustment_2026), at 4 (the revenue requirement "shall be allocated to all rate class groups by applying the Base Distribution Revenue Allocator," Residential 50.795%) (effective Feb. 1, 2026) [@nstarelectric_RevenueDecouplingAdjustment_2026]; [Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil, Revenue Decoupling Adjustment Clause (Schedule RDAC), M.D.P.U. No. 500](https://pub.switch.box/fge_RevenueDecouplingAdjustment_2026), at Sheet 4 ("The RDAF shall be calculated by comparing the difference between Annual Target Revenue to Actual Base Revenue for each rate class with the resulting differences summed to develop a total Company shortfall or surplus."), Sheet 6 (allocators approved in D.P.U. 26-39: RD-1/RD-2 61.18%, with HP-RES and HP-RES IE in the Residential group) (effective Nov. 1, 2026) [@fge_RevenueDecouplingAdjustment_2026].

[^8d-tsca]: National Grid, [Exhibit PP-8](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket2602Exhibit_2026), at 1 (single company-wide balance, ending Sept. 2025 under-recovery of `$44.4M`) [@meco_Docket2602Exhibit_2026], and [Exhibit PP-9](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket2602Exhibit_2026a), at 1, lines 2 (adding the under-recovery to the 2026 forecast), 5 and 6 (allocating the total by coincident-peak share, R-1/R-2 at 53.6%) [@meco_Docket2602Exhibit_2026a], both filed in D.P.U. 26-02; [National Grid, Transmission Service Cost Adjustment Provision, M.D.P.U. No. 1640](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket2671Exhibit_2026), at 1 ("The Company shall allocate the forecast of transmission costs and the balance of any over- or under-recoveries to its rate classes") (effective Nov. 1, 2026) [@meco_Docket2671Exhibit_2026]; Unitil, [Schedule SED-3](https://pub.switch.box/fge_Docket26154Schedule_2026), at 3, lines 4, 10 and 12–18, and [Schedule SED-4](https://pub.switch.box/fge_Docket26154Schedule_2026a), at 3, lines 18, 22 and 28–34 (prior-year reconciliation added to costs, then allocated to class groups by 12-CP; RD-1/RD-2 at 45.15%) (D.P.U. 26-154, filed Nov. 2, 2026; pending) [@fge_Docket26154Schedule_2026; @fge_Docket26154Schedule_2026a]; [NSTAR Electric, Transmission Service Cost Adjustment, M.D.P.U. No. 48A](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_TransmissionServiceCost_2025), at 1 ("a full reconciliation and adjustment for any over- or under-recoveries occurring under the prior year's adjustment") (effective Jan. 1, 2025) [@nstarelectric_TransmissionServiceCost_2025].

**What the DPU has done about it.** The DPU anticipated that shortfalls could occur and that they would run through decoupling.[^8d-expected] It now requires each company to report, in its annual decoupling filing, heat pump customers' billed revenue alongside what they would have been billed on the standard rate.[^8d-report] In NSTAR Electric's first report, its heat pump rate customers were billed \$10.3 million in base distribution revenue from their enrollment through April 2026, compared with \$33.2 million on the standard rate for the same usage.[^8d-nstar-report] That comparison overstates the revenue the company lost, however, because it mixes existing and new heat pump customers — both of which were and are auto-enrolled across the state — and only existing heat pump customers reduce revenue (CIEC-1(a)). New heat pump customers enrolled on the heat pump rate at the same time they increased their winter usage, so enrolling did not reduce the revenue they paid. In short, Massachusetts produces an estimate of the shortfall, and an overestimate at that, but recovers the shortfall entirely through its reconciling mechanisms, so part of it is paid by non-residential customers.

[^8d-expected]: D.P.U. 23-150, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket23150Order_2024), at 512 n.230 (Sep. 30, 2024) ("the Department expects there to be a reduced chance of significant revenue shortfalls . . . through the revenue decoupling mechanism") [@madpu_Docket23150Order_2024].

[^8d-report]: [D.P.U. 25-08-A Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2508Order_2026) at 2, 41 (directing the companies to report "the billed revenues recorded from heat pump customers in their annual revenue decoupling filings and to compare those revenues to the amounts that would have been billed if those customers had not enrolled in the heat pump rates") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

[^8d-nstar-report]: [NSTAR 2026 RDAF Filing](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket26143Revenue_2026) at 6 (billed winter base distribution revenue from each customer's enrollment through April 2026 of \$10,320,004 on the heat pump rate and \$33,211,094 on the non-heat pump rate; "[t]he underlying usage used for the revenue comparison is the same") [@nstarelectric_Docket26143Revenue_2026].

**How Rate HP improves on this.** Connecticut can learn from Massachusetts's experience in two ways. First, Rate HP plans for existing heat pump customers. When rates are set, the revenue they would no longer pay (for example, after a one-time mass auto-enrollment of Energize CT rebate recipients, as described in CIEC-1(a) and CIEC-1(b)) is built into Rate 1's rates, within the same rate class group (part (a) and CIEC-2(c)). The Massachusetts companies, by contrast, did not raise their standard residential rates to make up the revenue that the existing heat pump customers they auto-enrolled no longer pay. Second, for any shortfall that arises between rate cases, for example because enrollment differs from the forecast, I recommend that the Authority adopt Massachusetts's reporting requirement and go one step further: direct the Company to recover the shortfall from residential customers only (CIEC-2(d)). Together, these would keep Rate HP's effect within the residential class, a result the Massachusetts rates do not achieve.

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
The words "winter peak hour" in footnote 63 are a drafting error; they should read "summer peak hour."[^9a-n63] There are no winter peak hours on the Company's system today: no hour from November through March carries enough marginal distribution or transmission capacity cost to meet my testimony's definition of a peak hour.[^9a-peak] Rate HP's winter distribution rate reflects this. Because added winter usage causes almost no marginal distribution cost, the winter rate is set low enough that it adds little to a heat pump customer's bill.[^9a-calibrated]

[^9a-n63]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 59 n.63 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^9a-peak]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 16 n.9 (peak-hour definition), 17:1–3, 19:9–20:1 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^9a-calibrated]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
No, because the data needed for that analysis has not been made available to me.

First, there is no single level of adoption at which the Company's system becomes winter peaking. Each feeder and substation transformer has its own peak, and each would become winter peaking at a different level of heat pump adoption, depending on how many heat pump customers it serves and how much spare capacity it has. Today, the Company itself states that its system remains summer peaking.[^9b-summer-peaking]

Second, finding when individual feeders and transformers would become winter peaking requires their capacity ratings and their historical and hourly loads. CLF and Sierra Club asked the Company for exactly this information in CLF-SC-012 through CLF-SC-019.[^9b-requests] The Company designated it Critical Energy Infrastructure Information and will produce it only to parties that have signed a nondisclosure agreement with the Company.[^9b-ceii] CLF and Sierra Club have not yet reached mutually acceptable terms for that agreement with CL&P, so I have not received the data and have not been able to perform the analysis.

[^9b-summer-peaking]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-020](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 (Sep. 18, 2026) ("The Company currently does not use a heat pump forecast to inform its substation capacity projects as the system remains summer peaking.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

[^9b-requests]: Docket No. 26-05-10, [CLF and Sierra Club's First Set of Interrogatories to CL&P (Corrected)](https://pub.switch.box/clf_Docket260510Conservation_2026b), CLF-SC-12 to CLF-SC-19, at 8–14 (Sep. 4, 2026) [@clf_Docket260510Conservation_2026b].

[^9b-ceii]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-012](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1–2 ("highly confidential Critical Energy Infrastructure Information"; "the Company plans to supplement this response with production for all parties having executed an non-disclosure agreement with the Company, once an executed NDA is obtained from CLF-SC") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; _see also_ CL&P Responses to CLF-SC-013(a), at 2; CLF-SC-015, at 2; CLF-SC-016, at 1–2; CLF-SC-017(a), at 2; and CLF-SC-019, at 2 (same); CL&P Response to CLF-SC-014(a), at 2 (referring to the response to CLF-SC-012).

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
I recommend that Rate HP be recalibrated in each base rate case.[^9c-recalibrate] In each one, the Company would update its marginal cost study, basing the probability-of-peak analysis on actual substation and feeder loads, including heat pump load. It would then repeat the calculation in my testimony: set Rate HP's winter rates so that the average new heat pump customer pays their pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the marginal cost of their added load.[^9c-calibrated] Rate 1's rates would be reset at the same time, based on the customers who remain on Rate 1, so Rate 1's charges would account for existing heat pump customers who moved to Rate HP since the last rate case (CIEC-2(c)). Between rate cases, the Company would report heat pump customers' revenue as described in CIEC-8(d) and recover any shortfall from residential customers (CIEC-2(d)).

[^9c-recalibrate]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 7:9–12 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^9c-calibrated]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

I would support a requirement that Rate HP be recalibrated. I would _not_ support automatic expiry, because Rate HP is not justified only while the grid system remains summer peaking: it is justified for as long as Rate 1 charges heat pump customers more than the costs they cause.

A system that becomes winter peaking raises the costs that heat pump loads cause, but that alone does not make Rate 1's charges match them; what matters is how large those costs are. As feeders and substations become constrained in winter, winter loads would begin to drive distribution capacity investment. Recalibration would then move peak hours and marginal cost into winter, and Rate HP's winter rate would rise to match. Automatic expiry, by contrast, would end the rate as soon as the first feeders turned winter peaking, while heat pump customers as a group would still be paying far more than the costs they cause.

Today, Rate 1 charges the average converting household `{python} dollar(inc_td)` a year more in T&D charges, about `{python} num(td_to_mc_multiple)` times the `{python} dollar(inc_mc)` in added marginal cost it causes.[^9c-multiple] Even if the Company's entire system became winter peaking, and every hour of marginal capacity cost fell on the hours when heat pump homes use the most electricity, that added cost would rise to about `{python} dollar(c9.winter_peak_mc)` a year, and the household would still overpay under Rate 1 by about `{python} dollar(c9.overpay_remaining)`.[^9c-winter]

[^9c-multiple]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 23:3–5 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^9c-winter]: Illustrative calculation. I took the Company's hourly marginal distribution and bulk transmission capacity costs used in my testimony, sorted them from highest to lowest, and assigned them to the November–March hours ranked by the average converting home's electricity use after installing a heat pump, then multiplied each by the home's added load in that hour. This assumes every hour of marginal cost coincides with the hours when heat pump homes use the most electricity, so it overstates the cost: applying the same method to April through October gives `{python} dollar(c9.summer_check, 2)` a year, compared with the `{python} dollar(c9.inc_mc_testimony, 2)` from the testimony's hour-by-hour analysis. [CIEC-9 Attachment 1, `CIEC-9c_winter_peak_marginal_cost.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gXAdBUUKvNKrmlevgYMfACRsGwNv_jmX/view), sheet `hourly`: one row per hour in columns A–J, and the results as formulas in columns M–N. The `README` sheet explains each column [@velez_Docket260510CIEC9_2026].

::::{.part label="a."}
The modeled hourly electric resistance backup load[^10a-n4] for the average fossil fuel-heated home after heat pump installation[^10a-home] is provided in CIEC-10 Attachment 1, together with the home's hourly heat pump load and whole-home load, for all 8,760 hours of the modeled year, so the hours can be ranked by any of these loads.[^10a-att] Both the combined heat pump and backup load and the backup load alone would peak in the hour beginning `{python} c10_peak_hour` (Eastern Standard Time), when the home would use `{python} num(c10.peak_heating["heating_kwh"], 1)` kWh for heating, of which `{python} num(c10.peak_heating["backup_kwh"], 1)` kWh would be backup.[^10a-calendar] Over the year, backup would use `{python} num(c10.annual_backup_kwh)` kWh, or `{python} pct(c10.backup_to_heat_pump, 1)` of the heat pump's own `{python} num(c10.annual_heat_pump_kwh)` kWh.

Backup is ResStock's electric resistance element; heat pump load is the compressor and its supply fan.

[^10a-att]: [CIEC-10 Attachment 1, `CIEC-10a_hourly_backup_load.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Ls7qcRNn86aZyZYT53MyNmwt-Br3RCdr/view), sheet `hourly_load`: one row per hour in columns A–F, and the annual totals, backup ratio, and peak hours as formulas in columns H–I. The `README` sheet explains each column [@velez_Docket260510CIEC10_2026].

[^10a-calendar]: Hours are on the 2025 calendar used throughout the testimony ([Ex. JPV-3](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026), sheet `hourly_after` [@velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026]). ResStock models 2018 weather, shifted two days so weekdays line up; this hour reflects the weather of `{python} c10_peak_weather`. CIEC-10 Attachment 1 gives both timestamps for every hour.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
The `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` reflects the incremental heat pump load that actually causes new T&D costs: added cooling in summer, when the Company's feeders, substations, and the transmission system are closest to their capacity.[^10b-summer]

[^10b-summer]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 19:4–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

The same `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` holds in extreme cold, because heat pump and backup load in winter hours, however cold, does not add to that cost. A colder winter would raise the home's load in winter hours, but added load causes new T&D costs only when it pushes the system toward its capacity, and on the Company's system winter load is nowhere near capacity, even in very cold weather.

First, the Company's own loading data show large headroom at the summer peak. As I testified, "the typical feeder has 51% headroom even at its annual peak."[^10b-headroom] In its response to the data request, the Company did not identify whether these were summer or winter peaks,[^10b-season] but they are almost certainly summer peaks: the Company's own marginal cost witness found from its hourly substation loads that the Company "will continue to be summer-peaking through year 2031."[^10b-nieto] So headroom is already large in summer, and winter headroom is very likely even larger,[^10b-unavailable] because 82% of Connecticut homes heat with natural gas, fuel oil, or a fuel other than electricity.[^10b-winter]

[^10b-headroom]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 21:7–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]. The headroom is each feeder's most recent annual maximum loading (2025 where reported, otherwise 2024) as a share of its rated capacity, from the Company's response to System Data Requirement No. 2. _Id._ at 21 n.14.

[^10b-season]: _Id._ at 22:1–3 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^10b-nieto]: [Direct Testimony of Amparo Nieto, Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026d), at 6:9–12 (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026d].

[^10b-unavailable]: I requested each feeder's historical winter peak (Velez Direct at 22 n.15), but the Company will produce feeder and substation loads and ratings only under a nondisclosure agreement (CIEC-9(b)) that it has not yet signed; and it has not completed a winter peak forecast ([CL&P Response to CLF-SC-021](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c), at 1: "the Company is currently in the process of developing winter peak forecasts; however, these forecasts have not been fully completed") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026; @clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c].

[^10b-winter]: Velez Direct at 22:6–12 and n.17 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]. If some feeders' annual peaks were in winter, their winter headroom would still be at least what the testimony shows, because "the annual maximum is by definition higher than the winter peak alone." _Id._ at 22 n.16.

Second, this abundant winter headroom is reflected in the Company's marginal cost study, which found "a very small probability of peak falling on the coldest winter months."[^10b-mcos] Its probability-of-peak analysis is built from the Company's actual hourly substation loads for January 2022 through December 2025.[^10b-pop] Those loads include every heat pump and electric resistance heating system already on the system, and they cover the coldest hours of four winters. Even so, winter hours received almost no probability of being the peak. In other words, the electric heating load already installed, in the coldest weather of recent years, is too small to drive distribution capacity investment. The marginal bulk transmission costs come from the same method applied to New England system load for 2022 through 2025, and also fall in summer.[^10b-tx]

[^10b-mcos]: Nieto Direct, Exhibit CLP-MCOS-1, at 6:12–13 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026d].

[^10b-pop]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-033](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (reprinting the Company's response to OCC-733: "The sum of historical hourly Substation Loads from January 2022, to December 2025 across all the distribution substations provided by the Company were grouped by hour type") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

[^10b-tx]: Velez Direct at 15:6–16:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
The hourly calculation is in Ex. JPV-3, which was filed with my direct testimony in Excel format with formulas intact.[^10c-jpv3] Its `hourly_marginal_cost` sheet multiplies the average fossil fuel-heated home's load in each of the 8,760 hours, before and after heat pump installation (sheets `hourly_before` and `hourly_after`), by that hour's marginal transmission and distribution costs (sheet `marginal_cost`), and sums the results. Cell P4 gives the difference, `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` a year: `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_delta, 2)` in bulk transmission cost (cell P2) and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_delta, 2)` in distribution and sub-transmission cost (cell P3).

[^10c-jpv3]: [Ex. JPV-3](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026) [@velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026]. The hourly marginal costs are derived in [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 3, at 6–8 [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026].

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
ResStock's simulated loads closely match the Company's own residential sales. ResStock models a sample of homes, and gives each one a sample weight: the number of real homes it represents.[^11a-weights] I matched 3,539 of these modeled homes to the Company's service territory by location, then rescaled their sample weights so that, together, they represent the `{python} num(c11.rate_year_customers, 2)` residential customers the Company filed for the Rate Year. With that change alone, the modeled homes' total electricity use was only `{python} pct(c11_presale_gap, 1)` higher than the Company's Rate Year residential sales forecast of `{python} num(c11.rate_year_kwh)` kWh. I closed that gap by scaling every modeled home's hourly use, before and after heat pump installation, by `{python} f"{c11.kwh_scale:.3f}"`.[^11a-sales] Because each factor is the same for every home and every hour, neither step changes the shape of any home's load profile.

[^11a-weights]: [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 1, at 4 (Oct. 21, 2026) ("ResStock assigns each modeled dwelling a weight representing the number of real households it stands for.") [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026]. By design, each modeled home stands in for many real homes with similar characteristics.

[^11a-sales]: _Id._ at 4 ("For CL&P this factor was 0.995, a downward adjustment of roughly half a percent.") [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
The question is how the modeled fossil fuel-heated homes, which use an average of `{python} num(c11.fossil['Annual'])` kWh a year,[^11b-7211] compare with the Company's own customers who heat with natural gas, oil or propane. The Company has no usage figures for that group, because it does not track its customers' heating sources.[^11b-no-track] So the best available comparison is three indirect but complementary checks, each against data the Company does have:

[^11b-7211]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 8:1–2 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^11b-no-track]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-004](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 (Sep. 18, 2026) ("the Company does not track the heating sources of its customers") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

::::{.part label="a."}
Does Mr. Velez agree that the load of existing heat pump customers is already on the Company’s system and reflected in the sales used to set the Company’s rates in this proceeding? If not, explain why not.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Please identify any new load, or any reduction in the Company’s costs, that would result from enrolling existing heat pump customers in Rate HP.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Please provide Mr. Velez’s estimate of the annual reduction in distribution and transmission revenue attributable solely to the automatic enrollment of existing heat pump customers.

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
Please explain how the “pre-heat-pump T&D bill” referenced at page 85, lines 5-7 would be determined for an existing heat pump customer.

::::

:::

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
Yes. This is why I attribute the entire revenue reduction from Rate HP to existing heat pump customers, and none to new heat pump customers, who add load and revenue when they install (CIEC-1(a)). It is also why I recommend that the Authority set Rate 1 and Rate HP in this proceeding on billing determinants that already assign existing heat pump customers' load to Rate HP (CIEC-2(d)).

That their load is reflected in the sales used to set rates does not mean that their rates reflect the costs they cause. Under Rate 1, they overpay for T&D by an average of `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year (CIEC-1(a)).[^12a-overpay]

[^12a-overpay]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 23:9–10 (Oct. 21, 2026) ("fossil fuel-heated customers that install heat pumps overpay by an average of \$1,040 a year") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
None. When existing heat pump customers enroll in Rate HP, their usage does not change; they pay a lower winter rate on the same usage (CIEC-2(d)). The purpose of enrolling them is to end the overpayment described in part (a), not to change the Company's load or costs.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
As stated in CIEC-1(a), auto-enrolling the roughly `{python} num(existing_customers)` existing heat pump customers who received Energize CT rebates (CIEC-1(b)) would reduce the Company's revenue by about **`{python} million(short_existing['dist'])`** in distribution and **`{python} million(short_existing['tx'])`** in transmission a year, or `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` per customer. Tables 1 and 2 in CIEC-1(a) report this reduction separately from the revenue increase from new heat pump customers, in the "Revenue reduced" columns. If the Authority does not auto-enroll existing heat pump customers, I would expect the reduction to be an order of magnitude smaller (CIEC-1(a)).

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
It would not need to be determined. The pre-heat-pump T&D bill on page 85 is the _population-average_ bill of the modeled fossil fuel-heated homes, which I used to calibrate the rate: I found the single winter rate that makes their average T&D bill after installing a heat pump equal to that pre-heat-pump bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost.[^12d-calibrated] That one rate then applies to every enrolled customer, new or existing, without determining any individual customer's pre-heat-pump bill.

[^12d-calibrated]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–10 ("I found the single winter ¢/kWh rate that, applied to a sample of post-heat-pump load profiles, produces a population-average T&D bill equal to the customer's pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost"; "[b]ecause this is a single rate applied to all customers, it zeroes out overpayment _on average_") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

Charging only each customer's incremental heat pump load at its marginal cost, while ideal, would indeed require a baseline for each customer, and is not practical. As my testimony explains, there are three ways to set one, and each adds complexity. A separate meter on the heat pump would add cost and friction to enrollment, and rule out auto-enrollment entirely. Circuit-level energy monitors installed with each new heat pump could be compatible with auto-enrolling new customers, but not existing ones, and their savings would likely have to be delivered as credits by a third party rather than through the Company's bill. Billing software that estimates each customer's baseline from their past usage would avoid both problems, but only if the Company committed to building it.[^12d-thresholds] Because the first two approaches would make auto-enrollment difficult or impossible, they would lead to low enrollment and leave the cross-subsidy largely in place.[^12d-enrollment] I therefore propose a seasonal rate, which achieves largely the same result without a per-customer baseline.[^12d-seasonal]

[^12d-thresholds]: _Id._ at 79:14–81:4 ("There are at least three ways to implement per-customer thresholds."; "in order to achieve a block rate with per-customer thresholds that heat pump customers could be auto-enrolled into, the Company would either need to commit to a software-based solution, or to EnergizeCT contractors installing circuit-level energy monitors whenever they install heat pumps") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^12d-enrollment]: _Id._ at 80:16–18 ("The first two make auto-enrollment difficult to impossible, which would lead to single-digit rate enrollment and leave the cross-subsidy largely in place.") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^12d-seasonal]: _Id._ at 81:5–7 ("a simpler alternative to per-customer thresholds exists that achieves largely the same result: a seasonal rate design that lowers volumetric charges for heat pump customers in winter, without relying on a block threshold at all") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

::::

:::

## CIEC-13

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 7, lines 3-6, and page 93, lines 1-6.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 7, lines 3–6**

7:3    4. Auto-enroll all electric customers newly installing heat pumps into schedule Rate HP, at\
7:4        the time of installation. Customers would be identified through any existing or new\
7:5        programs that track heat pump adoption, while also offering an attestation and\
7:6        certification option for installation that may happen outside of these programs.

**Velez Direct, printed p. 93, lines 1–6**

93:1  **Every new customer that installs a heat pump** should be auto-enrolled in Rate HP at\
93:2  the time of installation. To achieve this, every customer receiving a heat pump incentive through\
93:3  Energize CT or the New England Heat Pump Accelerator should be placed on Rate HP\
93:4  automatically. For installations that happen outside of Energize CT — for example, self-funded\

::::{.part label="a."}
Please describe how Mr. Velez proposes that the Company verify that a customer enrolled in Rate HP has installed a heat pump and uses it as the customer’s primary source of space heating.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Would customers that use a heat pump only as a supplemental heating source, while retaining a fossil fuel heating system, be eligible for Rate HP? Explain.

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Would customers that heat with electric resistance, or that install ground-source heat pumps, be eligible for Rate HP? Explain.

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
Under Rate HP, would winter usage from end uses other than space heating, such as electric vehicle charging, receive the reduced winter rates? If so, please estimate the associated revenue reduction and explain why that result is consistent with cost causation.

:::

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
As proposed, Rate HP does not require that the heat pump be the customer's primary source of space heating. As my testimony states, Rate HP is for customers "who use a heat pump for heating."[^13a-who] Massachusetts uses the same standard: its heat pump rates are available to customers whose heat pump is used to "heat or supplement another heat source for their home or part of their home."[^13a-ma-avail]

[^13a-who]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 6:13–14 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^13a-ma-avail]: D.P.U. 25-55, NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, [Rate R-1HP, M.D.P.U. No. 85](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket2555Compliance_2025a), at 1 (Aug. 1, 2025) [@nstarelectric_Docket2555Compliance_2025a]; D.P.U. 23-80, Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil, [Response to DPU 2-04](https://pub.switch.box/fge_Docket2380Response_2023), at 1 (Sep. 19, 2023) (quoting the same language from Unitil's proposed tariff) [@fge_Docket2380Response_2023].

As for verification, my testimony proposes two channels.[^13a-channels] Customers who receive a heat pump incentive through Energize CT or the New England Heat Pump Accelerator are identified by the programs' own records and auto-enrolled. Customers who install a heat pump outside these programs submit "a simple form the installer or customer submits to confirm a qualifying heat pump was installed." I propose attestation to keep enrollment simple, as Unitil does in Massachusetts. Customers outside the efficiency programs enroll by contacting the company and "affirming that they are (or will) utilize their heat pump during the winter months." Unitil reviews each enrolled customer's usage annually.[^13a-unitil]

[^13a-channels]: Velez Direct at 93:1–6 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^13a-unitil]: D.P.U. 25-08, Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil, [Response to DPU-Common 3-5](https://pub.switch.box/fge_Docket2508Response_2026), at 1 (Jan. 23, 2026) [@fge_Docket2508Response_2026]; Unitil Response to DPU 2-04, at 1 ("The Company will review each customer on this rate annually to determine if the customer's usage is consistent with the use of a CCHP as the primary or supplemental source of heat.") [@fge_Docket2380Response_2023].

If the Authority prefers documentary verification for customers outside the incentive programs, it could follow Eversource and National Grid in Massachusetts. There, customers apply by phone, website, or mobile app, and provide "photos of equipment serial numbers; proof of payment or receipt of equipment purchase; or invoice or receipt from contractor installation." The utility may audit these documents and remove a customer whose documents cannot be confirmed.[^13a-docs]

[^13a-docs]: D.P.U. 25-55, NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, [Exhibit ES-HP-5, Residential Heat Pump Rate Implementation Plan](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket2555Residential_2025), at 4–5 (Apr. 17, 2025) [@nstarelectric_Docket2555Residential_2025]; D.P.U. 23-150, Massachusetts Electric Company d/b/a National Grid, [Exhibit HP-1, Residential Heat-Pump Rate Implementation Plan](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024), at 8–9 (Dec. 30, 2024) [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Yes. As explained in part (a), Rate HP is available to customers who use a heat pump for heating, whether or not it is their primary source of heat. The Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities has twice declined to limit its heat pump rates to customers with heat pumps sized to heat the whole home.[^13b-ma-ag]

[^13b-ma-ag]: D.P.U. 25-55, _Petition of NSTAR Electric Company, d/b/a Eversource Energy for Approval of Residential Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2555Order_2025), at 22 (July 29, 2025) ("Therefore, we decline to accept the Attorney General’s recommendation at this time.") [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025]; D.P.U. 23-80/D.P.U. 23-81, _Petition of Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil (Electric Division), pursuant to G.L. c. 164, § 94 and 220 CMR 5.00, for Approval of a General Increase in Base Distribution Rates for Electric Service and a Performance-Based Ratemaking Plan_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2380Order_2024), at 407 (June 28, 2024) ("we decline to limit the rate offering only to customers with heat-pump capacity sized to heat their entire home, as suggested by the Attorney General") [@madpu_Docket2380Order_2024].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
Customers who heat with electric resistance alone would not be eligible, because Rate HP is for customers who use a heat pump for heating.[^13c-who] An electric resistance customer who installs a heat pump would be eligible, like any other customer who installs one, "regardless of whatever heating system they had before."[^13c-prior]

[^13c-who]: Velez Direct at 6:13–14 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^13c-prior]: _Id._ at 81:15–16 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

Customers who install ground-source heat pumps would be eligible as proposed, as they are in Massachusetts.[^13c-ma-gshp] I did not analyze them separately: my analysis models air-source heat pumps,[^13c-ashp] and ground-source heat pumps account for only `{python} num(c13_gshp_installs)` of the `{python} num(c1.energizect_installations)` residential heat pump installations rebated through Energize CT since `{python} c1.energizect_years[0]`.[^13c-count] Because ground-source heat pumps are more efficient in cold weather, a customer who installs one would add less winter load than the average customer on whom Rate HP is calibrated. Such a customer likely overpays under Rate 1 as well, but by less, so the winter rate that would eliminate their overpayment would be higher than Rate HP's.

[^13c-ma-gshp]: D.P.U. 25-55 Order at 5 n.8 [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025].

[^13c-ashp]: Velez Direct at 10 n.4 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^13c-count]: Eversource Connecticut, [_Energize CT Heat Pump Installations, 2017 through November 2026_](https://pub.switch.box/clp_EnergizeCTHeat_2026), at sheets Detail and Export (downloaded Nov. 10, 2026) (residential space-heating installations by heat pump type) [@clp_EnergizeCTHeat_2026].

The Authority has three options for these customers: a separate rate that reflects their smaller overpayment; inclusion in Rate HP; or ineligibility. The case for inclusion rests on two points: there are so few of these customers, and their lower winter load helps limit the growth of winter peaks and the investment needed to serve them. No rate currently compensates them for that benefit.

::::

::::{.part label="d."}
Yes. Rate HP's reduced winter rates apply to all of an enrolled customer's winter usage. Applying them only to the heat pump's load would be ideal, but is impractical for the reasons given in my response to CIEC-12(d).

The revenue reduction from applying Rate HP to non-heating winter usage is already included in my estimates. Rate HP is calibrated on the modeled homes' whole-home load after installing a heat pump, including lighting, appliances, and every other end use. The single winter rate is set so that the average customer's T&D bill after installing a heat pump equals their pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost of the heat pump.[^13d-calibrated] The reduced rate on non-heating winter usage is therefore part of that calibration, and part of the revenue figures in CIEC-1(a).

[^13d-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

This is also why the result is consistent with cost causation. On average, Rate HP eliminates the overpayment without going past it: the average fossil fuel-heated customer who installs a heat pump still pays what they paid for their non-heating winter usage before installing the heat pump, plus the marginal T&D cost the heat pump causes.

The exception is electric vehicle charging. The ResStock load profiles I used do not include it, so I have not estimated the revenue effect of applying Rate HP's winter rates to it. Electric vehicles are still uncommon in Connecticut: at the end of 2025, plug-in and battery-electric vehicles made up about 3% of the passenger vehicles registered in the state.[^13d-ev]

A customer on Rate HP who charges an electric vehicle in winter would pay the lower winter rate on that charging too. But that is actually consistent with cost causation for the same reason as for heat pump load: on the Company's system, electricity used in winter causes almost no new T&D costs, because the system peaks in summer (see my response to CIEC-10(b)).[^13d-winter-mc] Even at Rate HP's winter rate, the customer would still pay more for that winter charging than the incremental marginal T&D costs that charging causes.

[^13d-winter-mc]: Velez Direct at 19:5 ("winter kWh carry near zero marginal T&D cost") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^13d-ev]: Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, [_EV Registration Factsheet_](https://pub.switch.box/ctdeep_EVRegistrationFactsheet_2026), at 2 (rev. Sept. 27, 2026) (73,156 battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, fuel cell and electric motorcycle registrations out of 2,305,954 passenger registrations on Dec. 31, 2025, or 3.17%, up from 2.69% on Dec. 31, 2024) [@ctdeep_EVRegistrationFactsheet_2026].

::::

:::

## CIEC-14

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 85, lines 1-19.

::: {.referenced-testimony}

**Velez Direct, printed p. 85, lines 1–19**

85:1   **Q. How did you determine the winter rate reductions for each component?**\
85:2   **A.** For each component — distribution and transmission — I asked: what reduction in the winter\
85:3   volumetric rate would make the annual overpayment of the _average_ fossil fuel-heated customer\
85:4   who installs a heat pump equal to zero? In other words, I found the single winter ¢/kWh rate that,\
85:5   applied to a sample of post-heat-pump load profiles, produces a population-average T&D bill\
85:6   equal to the customer’s pre-heat-pump T&D bill plus the incremental marginal T&D cost of\
85:7   serving the new electrified heating load.\
85:8   Because this is a single rate applied to all customers, it zeroes out overpayment _on_\
85:9   _average_ — individual customers with different load shapes will still have residual over- or\
85:10  underpayments. I address this issue below.\
85:11  **Q. A 71% winter reduction seems large. Why does the winter rate have to fall so steeply in**\
85:12  **order to eliminate the overpayment?**\
85:13  **A.** When one of the Company’s fossil-heated customers installs a heat pump, they cause only\
85:14  \$10 in incremental marginal T&D cost per year,[^77] on average, even though their winter\
85:15  consumption roughly quadruples, which causes their winter T&D bill to roughly quadruple as\
85:16  well. To satisfy cost-causation, the customer’s post-heat-pump winter T&D bill should\
85:17  approximately equal their pre-heat-pump-winter T&D bill, plus \$10. To achieve this, the winter\
85:18  rate has to drop by roughly the same factor that winter load goes up. Four times the kWh at a\
85:19  only slightly higher total bill means roughly one-quarter the rate per kWh — a ~75% reduction.

:::

::::{.part label="a."}
Please provide the derivation of the 71% winter distribution reduction and the 75% winter transmission reduction, including all inputs and calculations, in Excel format with formulas intact, to the extent not already provided in Exhibit JPV-4 or in response to CIEC-1.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
Please identify each element of the winter distribution and transmission rates (including any reconciling or rider components) to which the 71% and 75% reductions would apply.

::::

Please provide the resulting Rate HP winter rates in cents per kWh for each component.

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
The full derivation has already been provided in Ex. JPV-4, an Excel workbook with formulas intact, which builds on the hourly calculation in Ex. JPV-3 (see my response to CIEC-10(c)).[^14a-exhibits] For each component, I set the winter (November through March) rate so that the average fossil fuel-heated customer's annual delivery charges after installing a heat pump equal their delivery charges before installation plus the incremental marginal cost of serving the new load.[^14a-method] I describe the method in Ex. JPV-2, Section 5. The workbook works as follows.

[^14a-exhibits]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 7:13–18, 91 n.80 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [Ex. JPV-3](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026) [@velez_Docket260510JPV3_2026]; [Ex. JPV-4](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026) [@velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026].

[^14a-method]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 5, at 11–12 [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026].

The "monthly" sheet of Ex. JPV-4 holds the average fossil fuel-heated home's electricity consumption in each month before and after heat pump installation, along with the season of each month (winter is November through March). It also holds Rate 1's Distribution Energy Charge, net riders, Transmission Service Rate, and generation rate, and multiplies them into monthly charges. Rows 14 through 16 total those charges for the year, the winter, and the summer.[^14a-inputs] The "marginal_cost" sheet holds the home's annual marginal distribution and sub-transmission cost and marginal bulk transmission cost before and after installation, which are the totals in cells N2 through O3 of Ex. JPV-3's "hourly_marginal_cost" sheet, and the change in each (cells D3 and D4, which equal cells P3 and P2 of that sheet).

[^14a-inputs]: The average fossil fuel-heated home uses `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` kWh a year before installation and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_after)` after: `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_winter_before)` and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_winter_after)` kWh in November through March, and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_before)` and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_after)` kWh in April through October. Its incremental marginal cost is `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_delta, 2)` a year for distribution and sub-transmission, and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_delta, 2)` for bulk transmission. [Ex. JPV-4](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026), "monthly" sheet, cells C14 and D14 (annual) and rows 15 and 16 (winter and summer); "marginal_cost" sheet, cells D3 and D4 [@velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026].

The "rate_hp" sheet performs the derivation, in column B for distribution (riders included) and column C for transmission. Row 7 is the overpayment: the change in Rate 1 charges after installation (row 5) less the change in marginal cost (row 6). Holding summer charges at Rate 1 (row 9), row 12 solves for the winter rate that removes the overpayment: Rate 1's post-installation winter charges (row 10), less the overpayment, divided by post-installation winter kWh (row 11). Rows 13 and 14 confirm that summer charges plus the winter rate times winter kWh equal the home's pre-installation charges plus the change in marginal cost. Rows 18 through 23 restate the result as the Rate HP table in the testimony. Column E gives each winter rate's change from Rate 1: a `{python} pct(dist_cut)` reduction in the Distribution Energy Charge (cell E20) and a `{python} pct(tx_cut)` reduction in the Transmission Service Rate (cell E21).

The only inputs not calculated in Excel are the home's hourly loads and the hourly marginal costs in Ex. JPV-3. The code that produces them is identified in my response to CIEC-1 (Set CIEC-01), in the entries for the 71% and 75% figures.[^14a-ciec1]

[^14a-ciec1]: CLF and Sierra Club, _Responses to CIEC Interrogatories_ (PURA Docket No. 26-05-10), Response to CIEC-1 (Set CIEC-01) (Nov. 12, 2026), entries for Velez Direct at 6:19 and 7:1.

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
The reductions apply to two lines on the Company's proposed Rate 1 tariff, and only in November through March: the 71% reduction to the Distribution Service Rate charge per kWh (the Distribution Energy Charge), `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC)` per kWh, and the 75% reduction to the Transmission Service Rate, `{python} cents(FILED_TX)` per kWh.[^14b-tsr] The 75% reduction applies to the whole Transmission Service Rate, including the portion that reconciles the prior year's under- or over-collection, because the Transmission Adjustment Clause sets a single rate that covers both.[^14b-tac]

[^14b-tsr]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 82 (Table 4), 83:5–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^14b-tac]: Eversource Connecticut, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-3](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h), Transmission Adjustment Clause, at 409 (July 14, 2026) (the rate is "determined by dividing (1) the current period's Transmission revenue requirement; plus (2) a true-up of any under or over recoveries, including carrying charges, from the prior year's TAC charges or credits, by the kWh sales anticipated") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

Neither reduction applies to any other line on the Rate 1 tariff: the customer charge; the Electric System Improvements, Revenue Decoupling Mechanism, and Competitive Transition Assessment charges; the Systems Benefits Charge, Conservation Adjustment Mechanism, and Renewable Energy charge; the FMCC Delivery and Generation charges; or generation service.[^14b-sheet] The volumetric riders net to `{python} cents(FILED_RIDERS)` per kWh and stay at their Rate 1 levels.[^14b-riders] In the derivation, I solved for the winter distribution rate with the riders included, then subtracted the riders at their Rate 1 level, so the entire distribution reduction falls on the Distribution Energy Charge.[^14b-mechanics]

[^14b-sheet]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h) at 243–244 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

[^14b-riders]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 83:1–2, 83 n.74 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

[^14b-mechanics]: [Ex. JPV-4](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026), "rate_hp" sheet, cells B12 and D20 [@velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="c."}
In November through March, Rate HP's Distribution Energy Charge would be `{python} cents(hp_winter_dist_ec)` per kWh, compared with `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC)` under proposed Rate 1, and its Transmission Service Rate would be `{python} cents(hp_winter_tx)` per kWh, compared with `{python} cents(FILED_TX)`. The riders would stay at their net Rate 1 level of `{python} cents(FILED_RIDERS)` per kWh, so Rate HP's total winter delivery volumetric rate would be `{python} cents(hp_winter_total)` per kWh, compared with `{python} cents(FILED_TOTAL_DEL)` under Rate 1, a reduction of `{python} pct(1 - hp_winter_total / FILED_TOTAL_DEL)`. Summer (April through October) rates, the customer charge of `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, 2)` a month, and generation would be identical to Rate 1.[^14c-same]

[^14c-same]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 82:10–83:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [Ex. JPV-4](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026), "rate_hp" sheet, rows 18 through 23 [@velez_Docket260510JPV4_2026].

**Velez Direct, printed p. 98, lines 1–18**

98:1   charge would not approach the level needed to eliminate the heat pump cross-subsidy (\$121.49)\
98:2   for many decades to come.\
98:3   **Q. What about the tech-specific approach? What design levers does it offer, and why?**\
98:4   **A.** Within the default rate, where revenue sufficiency must be maintained, the only way to reduce\
98:5   overcollection from heat pump customers is to raise the fixed charge on everyone, shifting\
98:6   revenue recovery away from per-kWh rates.\
98:7   And the Company could choose to create a tech-specific rate exclusively for heat pump\
98:8   customers with a high fixed-charge design. Indeed, Rate 6 takes a step in this direction, by\
98:9   raising the fixed charge from \$12.36 to \$30.95.\

98:13  If the overcollection problem arises from the application of volumetric rates _designed for the_\
98:14  _average electric customer_ to a subclass of residential customers with structurally _above-average_\
98:15  usage, then simply lowering the volumetric rates for that population reduces overcollection from\
98:16  that population. Put another way, instead of fundamentally changing the rate design for Rate 1,\
98:17  you can simply recalibrate it, by designing the volumetric rate component for the average heat\

::: {.response}
::::{.part label="a."}
Exhibit JPV-2, Section 6 already gives the full derivation.[^15a-n85] CIEC-15 Attachment 1 reproduces it in Excel with formulas intact.[^15a-workbook] The derivation has two steps.

[^15a-n85]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 97 n.85 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; [Ex. JPV-2](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026), Section 6, at 13–14 [@velez_Docket260510JPV2_2026].

[^15a-workbook]: [CIEC-15 Attachment 1, `CIEC-15a_customer_charge.xlsx`](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1oxZKPR9bb3qG3r5ZXsRuGORi65zIlR-s/view). The `README` sheet lists the source of each input and explains each sheet [@velez_Docket260510CIEC15_2026].

First, I found how far Rate 1's distribution and transmission rates, including the distribution riders, would have to fall for the representative fossil fuel-heated home's overpayment to be zero. Under proposed Rate 1, those charges rise by `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_variable_charge)` a year when the home installs a heat pump, while its incremental marginal T&D cost is `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_marginal_cost)`. The rates would therefore have to fall to `{python} pct(fc.implied_lambda, 1)` of their filed levels, a cut of about `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)`. The customer charge does not enter this step, because the home pays it both before and after installing a heat pump.[^15a-step1]

[^15a-step1]: CIEC-15 Attachment 1, sheet `representative_home_bills`: the home's distribution and transmission charges before and after in rows 4–6, its marginal T&D cost in row 7, and the scaling factor in cell D8. The monthly kWh and rates they are computed from are on sheets `representative_home_consumption` and `rate_1` [@velez_Docket260510CIEC15_2026].

Second, I held Rate 1's revenue constant. At filed rates, distribution and transmission charges collect `{python} dollar(fc.class_variable_revenue_per_customer)` a year from each of Rate 1's `{python} num(fc.class_customers)` customers. Cutting them by `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` gives up `{python} dollar(fc.class_revenue_shift / 1e9, 2)` billion a year. Recovering that through twelve monthly bills raises the customer charge by `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge_delta, 2)`, from `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, 2)` to `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, 2)` a month.[^15a-step2]

[^15a-step2]: CIEC-15 Attachment 1, sheet `class` (Rate Year billing months and billed sales from Eversource Connecticut, [Exhibit CLP-RATES-2.4](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g) at 47 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g]), and sheet `modified_rate_1`: the revenue given up in row 4, the customer charge increase in row 6, and the redesigned customer charge in row 8. Rows 14–20 check that Rate 1's revenue is unchanged and that the home's overpayment is zero [@velez_Docket260510CIEC15_2026].

::::

::::{.part label="b."}
The redesign of Rate 1 in part (a), offered as an optional rate open to all residential customers, would do so. It would have a `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, 2)` monthly customer charge, distribution charges of `{python} cents(c15_dist_rate, 3)` per kWh and transmission charges of `{python} cents(c15_tx_rate, 3)` per kWh, with all other charges as in Rate 1.[^15b-rates] It would be revenue neutral in the sense I describe in my response to CIEC-2(a): if every Rate 1 customer took service under it, the Company would collect the same revenue it would under Rate 1 as filed. And for customers who take service under it both before and after installing a heat pump, it would eliminate the overpayment, for the reasons given in part (a).

[^15b-rates]: CIEC-15 Attachment 1, sheet `modified_rate_1`: the customer charge in row 8, the distribution rate (including riders) in row 22, and the transmission rate in row 23, each the filed rate times the scaling factor in part (a). Rows 14–16 check that it collects the same revenue as Rate 1 as filed [@velez_Docket260510CIEC15_2026].

- The New York Public Service Commission's Grid of the Future proceeding (Case 24-E-0165), where Switchbox's report _Heat Pump Rates in New York State_ (April 2026), which cites the Manual, was filed as Attachment 1 to a petition by Alliance for a Green Economy, Sierra Club, and other parties.[^19d-ny] The Commission has not acted on the petition.

  [^19d-ny]: N.Y. P.S.C. Case 24-E-0165, _Proceeding on Motion of the Commission Regarding the Grid of the Future_, [Petition of Environmental Defense Fund et al. to Advance Rate Design Supportive of Affordable, Beneficial Electrification](https://pub.switch.box/edf_Docket24E0165Petition_2026) at 4 n.1, 6 (May 5, 2026) [@edf_Docket24E0165Petition_2026].
